#5622. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5621. For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power.

Condo buyers today have more negotiating power than they’ve had in at least 13 years. There were an estimated 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in records dating back to 2013. The gap widened from 95.5% a year earlier.

Redfin estimates the number of buyers using proprietary data on the typical time between a buyer’s first home tour and the closing of a purchase, along with MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers is based on active listings in the MLS. The figures in this report are national estimates. See the full methodology and explore the interactive dashboard.

Redfin defines a buyer’s market as one with more than 10% more sellers than buyers, and a seller’s market as one with more than 10% more buyers than sellers. A market is considered balanced when the difference between sellers and buyers is within 10%. Other housing-market statistics, including median sale price, are based on Redfin’s analysis of MLS data.

A buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily mean condos are affordable for buyers.

The condo market has undergone a dramatic reversal since the pandemic-era homebuying boom. In September 2021, there were 25.1% fewer sellers than buyers.

Five years later, the number of buyers fell 54%, while the number of sellers rose 36%. The shift has left sellers competing for a much smaller pool of potential buyers.

The number of condo buyers fell to an estimated 88,460 in September, down 2.5 % from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, condo sellers totaled 197,248, up 0.9 % from the prior month.

Several factors are weighing more heavily on the condo market than on the single-family home market. Rising insurance premiums, HOA fees and special assessments are making condos increasingly expensive to own, particularly in Florida and Texas, where hurricane risks and other natural disasters have contributed to higher insurance costs. That’s a problem for first-time buyers, who often turn to condos as a more affordable entry point into the housing market but lack equity from a previous home sale.

While the condo market is challenging for buyers, those who can afford housing costs will have more power in negotiations.

“For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity,” said Asad Khan, a senior economist at Redfin. “Buyers have more options and a better chance of finding a place they like. Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes.”

The single-family market saw a similar trend in September, with the number of buyers dropping to a record low since 2013. Sellers outnumbered buyers by 53.7%–a wide gap, but less than half as wide as what we’re seeing in the condo market.

The huge surplus of condo sellers over buyers is contributing to the record-breaking buyer’s market in the overall housing market, which encompasses condos, townhouses and single-family homes

The national median condo sale price fell 0.8% to about $339,000 in September, the first year-over-year decline in five months.

House hunters should keep in mind that the costs of buying and owning a condo extend beyond its purchase price, and those ongoing expenses can put additional pressure on buyers’ budgets. Rising homeowners association (HOA) fees and insurance premiums can push up the total monthly cost of ownership. Buyers should also consider the possibility of special assessments to cover major repairs or improvements to a building’s common areas.

But for buyers who can afford the upfront costs of a condo and plan to stay put for several years, today’s buyer’s  market may offer an opportunity.

“Find a motivated seller and there are a lot of them,” said Cecilia Cordova, a Redfin Premier agent in Miami, who lives in a condominium herself. Researching the buildings you’d like to live in is the key to finding a financially healthy community and avoiding surprise assessment bills later, she said.

Condo buyers have more options than they did years ago. “We have enough inventory for the next three to four years,” said Cordova.

For prospective sellers? Cordova suggests considering renting their condo out for the time being. “If you really need to sell, the strategy is to list it lower than anybody else in the same building. It’s not time for you to try to experiment with a higher price,” she said.

Today’s home prices and mortgage rates have made it harder for first-time homebuyers to enter the market, reducing demand for condos, which have traditionally served as an entry point to homeownership. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.18% as of November 5, and home prices remain near historic highs.

Sellers are increasingly dropping their asking prices to attract buyers, Redfin data shows. About 37% of condos that sold in September had a price reduction, compared with 16% during the pandemic-era housing boom five years earlier.

The typical condo that sold in September spent 63 days on the market before going under contract, up from 35 days five years earlier.

Condo buyers in Texas had more negotiating powers than anywhere else in the country in September. San Antonio had the widest seller-buyer gap among the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas, with an estimated 459% more sellers than buyers. Houston followed with 322% more sellers than buyers, then came Austin, with 258% more.

Miami also had one of the nation’s widest gaps, with an estimated 274% more condo sellers than buyers in September, ranking third.

“San Antonio condos may have an attractive purchase price, but buyers are looking at the total monthly payment. Because we have so many affordable single-family homes available, many buyers choose a house when the payments are close,” said Derrell Skillman, a Redfin Premier agent in San Antonio, TX.

Skillman added San Antonio has a large military community, and its housing market tends to follow the military’s permanent change-of-station (PCS) season.

“We usually see more military-related activity during the spring and summer when families are transferring in and out of the area. Once that period slows down, the drop in demand can be more noticeable, especially in a smaller segment like condos,” he said. “HOA costs, financing restrictions, builder incentives, softer investor demand and the slowdown after the military PCS season are all contributing to the buyer’s market for condos,” said Skillman.

Meanwhile, new construction is adding to the softness in Sun Belt markets. The Sun Belt is home to nine of the 10 metros where condo sellers outnumber buyers most.

Nassau County, NY, was the only metro area among the 50 analyzed that was a seller’s market for condos in September. There were 32% fewer sellers than buyers, with an estimated 1,545 buyers compared with 1,052 sellers.

“Condo buyers are mostly people who want maintenance-free living,” said William Ortiz, a Redfin Premier agent in Long Island, NY. “They want to have an easier lifestyle as opposed to all the maintenance and upkeep that comes with a house. Common charges are expensive, but they’re willing to pay for that convenience.”

According to Sandra Glaser, a Redfin senior agent in Long Island, condo demand is coming from three main groups: first-time buyers priced out of single-family homes, particularly those moving from the city to the suburbs; downsizers seeking less upkeep; and investors looking for rental income from properties that require minimal maintenance.

Five other metros — Chicago, Milwaukee, New Brunswick, Newark and San Francisco — had balanced condo markets, where the difference between buyers and sellers was within 10%.

San Francisco’s condo market, for example, is heating up, with the median sale price jumping 20% year over year to nearly $1.2 million in September. Khan, the Redfin senior economist, ties the area’s renewed housing demand to the AI boom, which is attracting highly paid workers and fueling homebuying.

As a senior data reporter, Dian uses data and quantitative analysis to tell stories about economy and real estate. She also builds databases and creates statistical charts that visualize data trends. Previously, Dian spent seven years as a senior data reporter at USA TODAY.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5620. Court Report: Tuccori Settlements on Hold as Judge Requests Further Logistics

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

Tuccori settlement on hold after judge request

The approval of settlement agreements with more than 20 real estate companies in a major antitrust lawsuit filed by recent homebuyers challenging commission practices in the residential real estate market has been put on hold by a judge following a request for more information.

The settlements in the Tuccori v. At World Properties commission lawsuit were preliminarily approved back in May, but final approval has been put on hold as Judge Lindsay C. Jenkins has put in a request for additional information on five topics.

Firstly, Jenkins asked for clarification on a concern that was previously raised at a hearing: The valuation of claims filed, namely that “resolving 1/8 of all claims for 1/8 of what you paid to resolve the other 7/8 of all claims does not imply you valued the 1/8 and 7/8 equally on a per claim basis.”

Other requests include how each settler’s “ability to pay and transaction volume influenced their proposed settlement,” further information for the court to be able to arrive at the “net expected value of continued litigation,” benchmarks for “substantive adequacy from other indirect purchaser class actions,” and lastly, an estimation of per claimant and per class member recovery.

The National Association of Realtors®, one of the settlers in the case, said in a statement that it “continues to believe the Tuccori settlement is fair, reasonable, and in the best interests of the class.”

“The settlement offers meaningful protections across the industry, providing a broad release for REALTOR® members, REALTOR® associations, MLSs, and those brokerages that meet the settlement’s eligibility requirements,” the statement read. “NAR remains committed to fostering fair, transparent, and pro-consumer real estate markets while providing resources and value to our REALTOR® members nationwide.”

NAR added that the judge’s request is “a routine part of the class action settlement approval process, consistent with the judge’s role in evaluating the fairness of the settlement.”

“NAR is committed to abiding by the judge’s request to provide the Court with information in a timely and efficient manner, including working with the other parties, to demonstrate the settlement is fair and reasonable,” the statement concluded.

Briefs on the topics are due by Dec. 14, after which time the court will say if it needs further responses.

Fair housing lawsuit against Bank of America dismissed

A racial-discrimination lawsuit filed against Bank of America and a Virginia-based appraiser has been dismissed.

The suit was filed by Darchelle Braxton, a Black woman who last summer attempted to secure a loan for home improvements on an investment property. She claimed in her filing that an initial appraisal ordered by Bank of America valued her property at $135,000, but a subsequent second appraisal valued it more than 50% higher, at $208,000.

The appraiser—Velox Valuations—filed a motion to dismiss, refuting Braxton’s claims that it provided a “shockingly low” valuation on her property due to alleged “material errors, omissions, and inconsistencies,” which stemmed from racial bias. Such errors included allegedly using an incorrect map reference, using an incorrect neighborhood valuation, only using two comparable properties, inconsistent descriptions of the property’s condition, and more.

The suit was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

With the many legal battles the portal has faced as of late, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business” during its Q3 2026 earnings call.

CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann added that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

The portal is currently still facing a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5619. Hardware-testing and engineering startup Nominal raises $240M at $3B valuation

Artificial intelligence-powered hardware-testing and engineering software startup Nominal Inc. today announced it has raised $240 million in new funding led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners.

The investment triples the company’s valuation to $3 billion, up from $1 billion cemented in March after it raised $80 million in a Series B-2 funding round. Additional major investors in the Series C round included Lux Capital, Sequoia, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, Avenir, Salesforce Ventures, M13 and Lockheed Martin Ventures.

Nominal assists engineers with hardware development by supporting testing and development. Engineers must piece together data from disconnected testing systems to understand how a machine performed under realistic conditions and understand what needs fixing.

The platform brings that information together, automates testing, and uses AI to help analyze the results. This shortens the cycle between testing and design, enabling faster improvements and iterations.

The challenge in the field isn’t collecting more data; there are plenty of ways to get that from simulation, sensors, video, and more. Hardware tests generate streams of sensor readings, logs, video and simulation results that all need to be analyzed together to create a whole picture of what happened. The company’s AI agent, Nominal Analyst, investigates that data and performs analysis based on the underlying evidence.

“Hardware engineering is getting its AI moment, with real operational value that goes far beyond making existing workflows faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Cameron McCord. “The companies building the world’s most advanced machines have decades of hard-won knowledge in their organizations.”

The company said it built its AI Intelligence Platform to bring together all the systems needed for testing and design assistance. It has multiple layers, including connections to engineering applications, the agent infrastructure, the data and finally the physical world through sensors.

Examples of what Nominal’s AI product works with alongside engineers include aircraft, rocket engines, autonomous vehicles, drones and energy systems. Engineering data and documentation associated with the hardware fed to the agents help during the development process to investigate performance, compare tests and check results against requirements.

The company said the challenge is putting engineers’ knowledge to work and connecting it to data so engineers can take on harder problems than wiring up tests. The objective is to let them sit down, smooth out challenges and address what looked impossible before.

“Engineers stay in command, with purpose-built AI helping them do their best work,” added McCord.

Nominal works with the tools engineers already bring, including application programming interfaces, Model Context Protocol and SQL for database queries. Developers can also directly access the platform to connect tools, build custom applications, and create their own workflows and agents.

The company said more than 80 commercial and government organizations use its platform, including five of the seven biggest defense contractors. Nominal’s customers include defense technology company Anduril Industries Inc., military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls Industries Inc., known as HII, and high-speed aircraft developer Hermeus Corp.

#5618. VA Loans Can Open the Door to Homeownership 4 Years Sooner

When Thomas Couling, a young Air Force veteran, tried to buy his first home in the late 1970s, conventional lenders turned him away.

He had recently left the military, and his $11,287 annual salary as a rookie police officer in Michigan was barely enough to support his wife and newborn child.

"I could not afford to buy a home with that kind of wage," he tells Realtor.com®.

But a VA-backed mortgage gave him an opportunity that conventional financing couldn't. With help from his uncle, a contractor, and money borrowed from relatives to cover upfront costs, Thomas built his first home.

More than three decades later, his son, Coast Guard veteran Matt Couling, would turn to the same benefit to overcome a different obstacle: He had enough income to buy a home, but not enough savings for a substantial down payment.

Their experiences illustrate the findings of a new analysis from Realtor.com, which examines how Veterans Affairs loans can reduce the financial barriers to buying a home.

"At first glance, a 0% down VA loan costs about $20 more per month compared with a similar conforming loan requiring 10% down," explains Jiayi Xu, Realtor.com senior economist and author of the report. "But it saves $41,925 upfront, which cuts the time to homeownership by around four years."

Those savings are perhaps the biggest benefit of the VA loan program, because they address the biggest hurdles to homeownership head-on.

Roughly 11% of renter households under 40 have sufficient income to afford a median-priced home but lack the savings for a 10% down payment, according to the Realtor.com analysis of Federal Reserve consumer finance data.

Meanwhile, the median age of first-time homebuyers remains at a record 40, and their share of home purchases sits at just 22%, according to the National Association of Realtors®' latest report.

And those who are breaking in are relying on family help more than ever before. One-quarter (25%) of first-time buyers received gifts or loans from family and friends toward their down payment, according to NAR.

But many would-be buyers can’t count on that kind of family support—just like Matt couldn’t when he purchased his first home near Portland, ME, in 2011.

"The zero money down aspect of the VA loan is really what allowed me to buy my first house," he says.

Over the past year, 75.7% of VA-financed home purchases required no down payment whatsoever, while 86.1% involved down payments below 10%. By comparison, just 41.1% of home purchases financed with conforming mortgages had down payments below 10%.

But the benefits of VA loans don’t stop there. Between October 2025 and September 2026, the average rate on 30-year fixed VA purchase loans was 5.81%, compared with 6.22% for conforming loans.

When both borrowers put 10% down on a median-priced home, the analysis finds that the VA borrower would save approximately $261 monthly, or more than $3,100 annually.

The program also offers borrowers with less-established credit greater flexibility. Nearly one-quarter (24.3%) of recent VA borrowers had fair credit scores, compared with just 4.8% of conforming borrowers.

After about eight years in his first home, Thomas sold it and used the proceeds to help finance another house in the Michigan countryside, where he raised his family.

"Probably without the VA loan, we would have had to rent for several years," he says. Also, they likely wouldn't have accumulated the money needed for their next purchase.

He's speaking to perhaps the biggest long-term advantage that homeownership offers: Each additional year gives owners more time to pay down mortgage debt and potentially benefit from rising property values.

So the earlier you get in, the more room you have to benefit.

Earlier research from Realtor.com found that households buying their first home between ages 28 and 32 had approximately 22.5% more net worth by age 50—equivalent to $119,000—than comparable households that waited until their 40s.

Matt would also discover the value of having access to the benefit at another pivotal moment in his life.

After retiring from the Coast Guard and experiencing a significant financial setback, he wanted to establish a permanent home for his children in Celebration, FL, where he was working for Disney. But the local housing market presented another obstacle.

"While I had recovered some savings at the time, I didn't have sufficient savings to put 20% down on a million-dollar house," he says.

So he used his VA benefit for a second time and was able to purchase the home without exhausting the savings he had rebuilt.

He describes it as far more than a financial investment.

"The availability of the VA loan made buying a house something that I could do, a gift I could give to my children that I otherwise would not have been able to do," he says.

But military service can present its own challenges to becoming a homeowner, even with access to favorable financing.

Active-duty military personnel have substantially lower homeownership rates than the general population, despite higher incomes and educational attainment, according to a 2024 Urban Institute study. Researchers identified frequent moves and younger ages as the two largest contributing factors.

Matt, who retired as a Coast Guard command master chief, says military life often encourages service members to think about their finances in much shorter increments.

"You're basically living two or three years at a time," he says, citing deployments, duty stations, and promotions shaping financial planning.

That short-term focus can make it harder to plan for a home purchase, particularly when service members don't know how long they'll remain in one location.

Awareness is another issue: 68% of current and former service members were unsure or incorrect about whether VA loans required a down payment, according to 2026 survey commissioned by mortgage lender NewDay USA.

Thomas knew about VA mortgages when he left the Air Force, but there was one advantage he didn't discover until years later: The benefit can be used more than once.

"I thought it was a one and done deal," he says.

The Department of Veterans Affairs reiterated in September that eligible borrowers can use the benefit repeatedly, provided they meet applicable lending and occupancy requirements.

Thomas says he would have considered using the benefit again when buying his second home, had he known it was an option. His son, meanwhile, has now used it three times.

"I didn't have 10 years of planning behind that," Matt recalls of his first purchase. "The VA loan allowed me to do that."

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5617. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5616. Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of a Big Week for Inflation Data

In A Nutshell:  Mortgage rates are coming down as investors dial back expectations for rate hikes. But that could change: Key inflation data comes out this week.

Two highlights from a busy election week:

This week’s economics highlight is the CPI inflation data coming Tuesday, coupled with Friday’s PPI data. Together, the two will form a complete picture of the core PCE inflation measure the Fed uses. The consensus forecast has core CPI coming in at 0.2% month-over-month, down slightly from last month. Forecasters are expecting a small statistical distortion in the data due to last year’s government shutdown. A very low read for inflation might convince the Fed to hold off on hiking rates at the December meeting, but they could just as easily write it off as one data point. They would evaluate how broader financial conditions have changed since the last meeting, including any further improvement in rates.

Many Fed officials are holding speaking engagements this week. The ones to watch are Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on Tuesday; Vice Chair Michelle Bowman on Monday, Tuesday, and Friday; Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday; and New York Fed President John Williams on Thursday.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5615. A Tuskegee Airman’s Legacy of Generational Wealth—and His Granddaughter’s Mission to Expand It

Julia Lashay Israel bought her first home at 19, never considering it a remarkable achievement.

Only decades later did she begin tracing that sense of possibility to a VA mortgage her grandfather, one of the original Tuskegee Airmen, secured after World War II.

"We never talked about the house. We always talked about the Tuskegee Airmen," Israel tells Realtor.com®.

Her family's experience stands apart from that of many Black Americans. Just 44.4% of Black households owned their homes in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 75.1% of non-Hispanic white households, according to Realtor.com research.

Israel, now a real estate broker and educator, has spent years teaching agents about the discriminatory housing policies that helped create that divide—and how their own practices can perpetuate it.

Ahead of Veterans Day, she shared her grandfather's story at the National Association of Realtors® NXT conference in New Orleans, illustrating what access to homeownership could make possible for generations of a family.

Israel's grandfather Sgt. Morrissey Whitley was just 20 when he entered the military aviation training program in Tuskegee, AL, in 1942—eventually serving in intelligence as a draftsman for the 332nd Fighter Group, according to Israel.

Just a year earlier, the U.S. Army Air Corps had begun admitting Black men after decades of exclusion, following pressure from civil rights organizations.

But the training program remained segregated, and the Tuskegee Airmen faced hostility, unequal treatment, and military officials who questioned whether Black servicemen were capable of flying combat missions.

Despite those systemic obstacles, the Tuskegee Airmen distinguished themselves in combat, helping challenge the racist assumptions that had excluded Black Americans from military aviation.

Whitley made sure his descendants understood their achievements, too.

When Israel told him an elementary school teacher had claimed Black Americans hadn't served in WWII, he assembled a folder of evidence for her to take to class.

But the racial barriers facing Black servicemen didn't end when they returned home.

And in the housing market, those divisions were reinforced by redlining, which restricted where Black families could obtain mortgages—and, ultimately, where they could build wealth.

In 1940, just 22.8% of Black households owned their homes, compared with 45.6% of white households, according to historical U.S. Census Bureau data.

And even while the GI Bill subsequently helped millions of returning veterans purchase homes through government-backed mortgages, lenders often refused to finance properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods.

On top of that, racially restrictive covenants excluded Black buyers from many white neighborhoods.

As a result, just 5.1% of VA-guaranteed loans in an early federal mortgage sample went to Black borrowers, according to a 2026 study published in Nature.

Whitley was among those who secured financing, purchasing a home in Gary, IN, after moving his family from Chicago, according to Israel—a move that she believes was made necessary because of discriminatory lending practices.

"You can't use your VA loan in Chicago," she says. "You have to live where Black people are redlined to live."

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Israel developed a course teaching real estate agents about the history of housing discrimination—including redlining, restrictive covenants, and the industry's role in perpetuating segregation.

She later taught it through Keller Williams' social equity task force, established after George Floyd's killing in 2020. Her training has since reached more than 40,000 agents, according to NAR.

What surprised Israel was how many agents were unfamiliar with that history—or how their own decisions could perpetuate its consequences.

"There's been different buyers, different sellers," she says of the persistence of residential segregation. "The only common denominator is the Realtor®."

Israel has witnessed discrimination firsthand.

"I've had people not sit in closings with us because we were Black," she says, recalling a Minnesota home closing in the mid-2000s.

Black applicants were 7.8 percentage points more likely than white applicants to be denied mortgages, even after accounting for financial characteristics and lender differences, according to a 2026 Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis study.

Israel also worries about agents discouraging buyers from pursuing certain financing programs or directing them toward particular neighborhoods without considering the long-term consequences.

Her courses emphasize the importance of understanding those barriers and earning buyers' trust, particularly when they're navigating a process nobody in their family has experienced before.

During 13 years working primarily with first-time buyers, many of them Black single women, she encountered clients who were hesitant to sign agreements or trust the professionals guiding them.

"A lot of times they are the first, and so if you're the first person who's ever done it, yeah, that's pretty scary," she says.

Israel grew up with a very different understanding of homeownership.

"My grandparents always had a house. My parents always had a house," she says.

In fact, she remembers envying classmates who lived in apartment complexes, where they could play together after school.

Her own children inherited that familiarity. Israel recalls her young son accompanying his grandmother to look at a rental apartment and repeatedly asking, "When's the closing?"

He couldn't understand why someone would pay to live in a home they didn't own.

It wasn't until Israel began working in real estate that she recognized how her family's experience differed from that of many neighbors and fellow churchgoers who rented their homes.

That early exposure can have lasting consequences. Children who grew up entirely in homeowner households were 18.4 percentage points more likely to become homeowners themselves by age 35 than those raised entirely in renter households, according to Realtor.com research.

Housing-related financial advantages can also persist across generations independently of what children earn themselves. Less than half of the persistence in housing capital across generations is explained by children's earnings, according to a 2025 U.S. Census Bureau study examining more than 3.4 million families.

Those advantages have been distributed unequally. Median white family wealth stood at approximately $332,100 in 2025, compared with just $36,800 for Black families, according to a Tax Policy Center analysis of Federal Reserve data.

Israel's own family never had substantial financial resources growing up, despite their history of homeownership.

"We never had a lot of money, but we always had a lot of sense," she recalls.

And when her granddaughter was born, Israel began reconsidering how far the opportunity her grandfather secured had carried the family.

"He didn't leave us any money, but he left us, like, a legacy," she says.

It was that realization that prompted Israel to begin incorporating Whitley's experience into her educational work.

"It's really not about quartz countertops or, you know, the cute fence," she says of the work real estate agents do. "It really is that we're planting seeds for families."

Her own grandfather had planted one more than eight decades earlier. And now, another generation of his descendants is benefiting from the opportunities that followed.

"This little baby is a trust fund baby, and she'll never know that it was because her great-great-grandfather had an opportunity that other people didn't have that set the path of this legacy for her," Israel says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5614. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5613. On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging

The very blue results of last week’s midterms have sent technology investors into a tailspin.

With many successful candidates running on platforms opposing data centers and calling for greater restrictions on artificial intelligence, investors anticipate a slowdown in AI spending. Tech stocks fell, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5.5%.

“Yesterday was a bloodbath,” said John Furrier (pictured), executive analyst for theCUBE Research. “It was brutal here and the tech stocks got pounded. 41 states had data centers on the ballot. They all lost or won, depending how you look at it. Now it’s so mainstream, it’s a political football. So you’re starting to see the reality of AI. It’s hitting everybody. Everyone is impacted.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed the fallout from the midterms and whether or not AI companies will really suffer in the long term. They also explored who will own the “system of intelligence” that will govern enterprise AI.

After the “bloodbath” last week, the question remains: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Despite the shockwaves from the midterms, theCUBE’s researchers are predicting a longer path toward monetization. A recent analysis identified 2029 as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble.

“There’s a clock in terms of the data center monetization and financing and how long it takes to build data centers,” Vellante said. “We know anybody who can sell GPUs is making money but the enterprises aren’t yet self-funding. I had said that by 2026, this year, you’re going to start to see clear evidence of monetization in the enterprise. I think you see it, but you’re seeing it within tech companies.”

Tech companies are applying AI more effectively, according to Vellante, which should not come as a surprise. He thinks the tech titans are in a solid position while neoclouds are taking on a greater share of risk by pioneering a new software model, although not all of them will make it in the long term.

A GPU-based AI economy will shift in the next several years, Furrier believes, which could lead to surprising winners and losers.

“Supermicro [Inc.], good numbers, [Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Arista Networks, Marvell Technology Inc.],” he noted. “My take is this: the infrastructure is evolving beyond GPU-centric computing. Networking, optics, memory, storage, power efficiency. System-level architecture is becoming the strategic advantage, and those bottlenecks are being solved by the companies I just mentioned. You saw the news that Marvell closed a $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum.”

The stock market plunge shows that not everyone is going to make it through the AI era’s eventual slowdown. Public opinion on data centers is mixed, to say the least, so companies will need to establish a foothold in the developing system of AI intelligence to remain competitive.

“Neoclouds like CoreWeave are going to make it through,” Vellante said. “They’re the first movers and they’ve got some quality advantages but they’re going to go through some pain. Hyperscalers are like an ATM. They could dial it down at any point in time … but right now it’s all about growth, it’s about footprint, it’s about market share.”

Who owns the “system of intelligence”? This layer, which will bridge the gap between intelligent agents and the data systems they depend on, appears to still be in play. Palantir Technologies Inc. has the ontology that could give it the edge, while Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. are still developing the operational systems — though Vellante sees the latter as having one of the best strategies.

“You need determinism to own that system of intelligence,” Vellante said. “So I think it’s wide open. Right now, I think Ali Ghodsi [chief executive officer of Databricks] has the best vision. He’s going after the client surface, he’s going after the system of intelligence, he’s going after the governance catalog, he’s going after the agent action layer, and he’s partnering … with all the frontier model vendors. Whether or not they can pull it off, we’ll see.”

Frontier models are the “wild card,” as Vellante puts it, but at the moment, all the tech companies are trying to get a slice of the pie. Despite the recent market shakeups, Furrier sees AI-native enterprises as the ultimate result of this current period of growth.

“The AI-native enterprise or businesses is going to be the model,” Furrier said. “Everybody wins in that one. Compute providers, hyperscalers, the data platforms that are on the right side, and the application companies, which are basically going to be agentic. That’s going to be the winners on the profit concentration. The control point … it’s not going to be the models, it’s going to be data and context, and the agents will be the proof point.”

Tom Lee, investor and entrepreneur Dan Ives, technology analyst Frank Slootman, former chairman of the board of directors at Snowflake Inc. #5612. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.

#5611. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.
