#5580. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5579. California voters reject measure to shred environmental red tape

California voters voted down Proposition 45, which sought to speed CEQA environmental reviews through standardized deadlines and faster court timelines. The measure lost 56% to 44% in unofficial returns, and the streamlining fight is expected to return to the Legislature.  AI Summary

California voters have rejected a ballot measure to speed environmental review of housing and other projects.

Proposition 45 would have consolidated a patchwork of legislative fixes to the California Environmental Quality Act, aimed largely at reducing a costly hurdle to building housing. The Associated Press called the race over the weekend, though the state is still counting votes. Unofficial returns showed about 56% of voters opposed and 44% in favor, a spread too large to overcome with the remaining votes.

It failed decisively across populous coastal counties, where housing affordability is a pressing concern. Voters in Santa Cruz, Marin and Sonoma counties rejected the measure by the widest margins.

Opponents tied the measure to data center development, an influential argument in midterm races nationwide.

“Californians have sent a clear message to corporate developers, utilities and data center builders that they will not stand for a broad assault at the ballot box on state law protecting our air, water and natural resources,” the Vote No on Prop 45 campaign released in a statement.

Proponents dubbed that an inaccurate scare tactic.

“The opposition relentlessly lied, falsely claiming that Prop 45 covered data centers when non-partisan experts agreed it did not – and used smokestack images and scare tactics about air and water pollution when the ‘essential projects’ included in Prop 45 did not include smokestack industries and also excluded mining, port, and other controversial projects,” Jennifer Hernandez, who leads Holland & Knight’s West Coast land-use and environmental group, told HousingWire TBD.

Opponents also countered the claim that the measure would help create affordable housing. They cited housing groups that urged a no vote or declined to endorse. Abundant Housing LA and California YIMBY, both of which endorsed L.A. Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, did not endorse the measure.

Opponents included the California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters and the American Lung Association. Sierra Club California and the California Federation of Labor Unions also opposed it.

The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored the measure, with backing from home-builder groups and some affordable housing advocates.

“We were outspent but not outgunned, thanks to a broad bipartisan coalition that understood that Californians know we can have progress and safeguard our environment at the same time,” the campaign noted in its statement.

Had it passed, the measure would have capped full environmental impact reports at 365 business days. Court challenges would have faced a 270-day limit.

Covered “essential” projects included housing, water, energy, schools, health facilities and transportation. Applicants could have chosen the new procedures or the existing ones.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office said the measure could cost local governments up to $100 million a year at first. Long-term financial effects were unclear. A Chamber-commissioned analysis projected $1.5 billion in savings and added revenue over 10 years.

Prop. 45 followed a run of legislative changes that limited CEQA reviews of housing proposals. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131 in 2025. They exempted qualifying infill housing from CEQA and narrowed review for some projects falling short of an exemption.

A newer round of bills signed this fall targets more permitting delays. Some shield specific developments from further CEQA challenges. One is a major mixed-use development in San Diego.

Backers argued those fixes helped only some projects. They said project-specific exemptions left other developments exposed to years of delay. Prop. 45 would have applied common deadlines to all eligible projects.

Supporters said predictable timelines would help California build homes and the infrastructure that serves them. They said CEQA lawsuits add tens of millions of dollars in costs, and thwart efforts to increase housing supply by escalating entitlement risk. They also argued that the measure could cut delays by two to 10 years.

“Not-in-my-backyard” and environmental groups have long sued local governments under CEQA. Those suits typically argue agencies did not properly handle environmental impact reviews.

A study by Hernandez and other researchers reviewed 498 CEQA appellate decisions from 2013 through 2023. Agencies prevailed in 75%. But the study said prolonged litigation still stalls financing and raises costs. It covers appellate decisions only and predates the 2025 reforms.

Opponents said the 2025 reforms already addressed much of CEQA’s housing problem. They said Prop. 45 would cap public-comment periods, narrow tribal consultation and limit judicial review. They also argued that affordability was being used as cover for a developer advantage.

Critics said “essential” was defined so broadly that it could fast-track freeways, power plants and pipelines.

The fight to streamline CEQA may now shift back to the Legislature and a new governor.

“We know this fight is not over,” the No on Prop 45 campaign wrote in its statement.

“The good news is that many millions of Californians voted for Prop 45, and do want timely, accountable, and predictable outcomes in CEQA,” Hernandez said. “Our legislative supporters saw the dirty trick campaign tactics unfold, and now have the opportunity to adopt these important CEQA reforms for the ‘essential projects’ that California needs to restore affordability to our state.”

#5578. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5577. Five FAQs homeowners have about private flood insurance

Private flood insurance is gaining attention as flooding shifts beyond mapped zones. Here are five common questions on coverage, NFIP differences, how private and NFIP policies can work together, eligibility and what homeowners policies typically exclude.   AI Summary

Extreme weather events caused by El Niño are dominating today’s headlines, driving an increased interest in flood insurance. However, flood patterns across the U.S. have been changing for years, even before El Niño. For example, catastrophic flooding is no longer dominated by events located in traditional flood zones or near coastal waters, but instead is increasingly defined by heavy rainfall.

As flood risks evolve, more homeowners are turning to private flood insurance – an alternative to coverage through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). For real estate agents guiding their clients through the home buying process, here is some basic information that clients need to know about this option.

Private flood insurance is a risk management tool backed by global capital markets that provides financial protection for buildings and personal property damaged by floods, helping families, communities and businesses to recover from these devastating events.

The primary difference between an NFIP and a private policy is the source of capital.

With an NFIP policy, FEMA holds all program risk, with United States taxpayers serving as the ultimate backstop. With private flood insurance, independent insurance companies bear the risk of loss. As a result, these companies leverage global capital structures to support risk selection and risk management in order to deliver a sustainable program capable of responding to customer needs.

While private insurers cannot be all things to all people, this disciplined and thoughtful approach means these insurers can deliver a sustainable and valuable product to their customers.

A private policy can act as either an alternative or a complement to an NFIP policy. Private policies equip agents with customizable options that can cater to individual homeowners’ needs, allowing insurance agents to craft solutions that ultimately help protect more people from floods.

Private policies can also complement an NFIP policy. If you have an NFIP policy, you can purchase private insurance to increase coverage beyond the limits offered by the federal program. Private insurance is also available to expand coverage, such as adding protection for contents in a basement or the expense to clean out a swimming pool.

The NFIP is essentially a one-size-fits-all policy available to almost every person in all geographies. However, the reality is that all homeowners aren’t the same. That’s the beauty of private insurance programs; they’re flexible programs that can respond to the individual needs of customers, like high-net-worth homeowners or renters.

Generally speaking, most homeowners’ policies exclude flood losses. A homeowners’ policy may cover water damage from broken pipes or sump pumps, but most exclude loss from inundation, whether resulting from swollen rivers, storm surge or intense rainfall.

The flood insurance industry is rapidly changing, and there are new opportunities coming online every day. To make the best decisions for clients, every real estate agent should take time to understand these new options.

In most situations, the home is the family’s most valuable investment. Wherever it rains, it can flood, so take time to consider solutions that can protect these treasured investments from catastrophe.

#5576. Meta introduces Muse Ember to power cost-efficient AI agents

Meta Platforms Inc. today introduced Muse Ember, an entry-level artificial intelligence model that costs significantly less than the competition.

Notably, it’s the first AI that the company trained using Muse Wonder. The latter algorithm is the Facebook parent’s flagship large language model. Meta didn’t specify which part of the workflow it automated with Muse Wonder.

One possibility is that the company used it to perform post-training, the task of honing a model’s capabilities by training it on additional data. Thinking Machines Labs Inc. recently demonstrated that even a relatively small LLM can run post-training runs end-to-end. Anthropic PBC, for its part, last week revealed that its AI models could soon gain the ability to significantly accelerate machine learning research.

Applications often use frontier LLMs such as Muse Wonder as part of AI ensembles. When a user enters a request, the frontier LLM splits it into smaller tasks and assigns them to agents powered by a lower-cost model. Meta says Muse Ember is specifically optimized to play the latter role.

The company evaluated the model using the Artificial Analysis Index, which aggregates nine AI benchmarks spanning use cases such as coding and financial analysis. Meta says that Muse Ember matched the score of Anthropic’s entry-level Claude Haiku 5.5 model at about a third the price. It also outperformed OpenAI Group PBC’s comparable GPT-6 Luna algorithm.

The same internal evaluation saw Meta test Muse Ember and the two rival models across nine other benchmarks. All three algorithms were in “max” mode, which means they used the maximum amount of hardware at their disposal instead of prioritizing cost-efficiency. Muse Ember outperformed Haiku and Luna across seven of the benchmarks.

The area where the model appears to have the biggest edge is business task automation. Whereas most of Muse Ember’s benchmark results were only a few percentage points better than those of Haiku and Luna, it clocked a 17% lead on AutomationBench-AA. It’s a collection of 657 tasks that span popular cloud applications such as Gmail and Salesforce.

Muse Ember has a context window of 1 million tokens, which enables it to ingest lengthy business documents. Users can also include images, audio and video in their prompts. The model generates responses up to 512,000 tokens in length.

Muse Ember is available through Meta’s Model API for 10 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens. A built-in cache can reuse frequently used prompts to avoid duplicate processing. When the feature is active, Muse Ember’s pricing drops to 0.4 cents per million input tokens.

#5575. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5574. AI is already in real estate, and its next opportunity is connection

Surveys show broad AI use across real estate and title. The next opportunity is connecting data across systems so teams can answer file status, reduce re-entry and route tasks with clear review and permissions.  AI Summary

In real estate, a simple customer question can send a professional searching across several systems: “Where is my file?” AI’s next opportunity is to help bring the answer into view.

Imagine being able to answer that question with the relevant information already in view. The order, the outstanding requirements and the next steps would be available to the person helping the customer. That is an exciting prospect for an industry where getting an answer can still mean checking several systems and making a few calls.

For real estate and title, AI becomes more useful when it can reach the information people need to do their jobs.

We already have momentum. In a Realtors Property Resource survey of 225 real estate professionals, 82% of respondents said they use AI in their business, commonly for listing descriptions and emails. Qualia’s 2025 survey of 631 title and escrow professionals found that nearly 90% of respondents use at least one AI tool.

People are putting AI to work. Now we have an opportunity to connect that work across the transaction.

A connected workflow could draw on information from across the transaction. Think about what that could mean for a title professional answering a customer, an underwriter reviewing a file or a manager deciding where a team needs help.

Of course, real estate has its own complications. A title file depends on agents, lenders, underwriters, public records and production systems. Requirements vary locally. Acquisitions bring together companies with different technology and processes. Connecting that environment takes work, but the benefits show up in very practical places.

Start with a field conversation. Relationships drive this business, and representatives learn valuable information while talking with agents and referral partners. Capturing activity from a phone while it is fresh could help teams schedule follow-ups and give colleagues a shared view.

Picture that information reaching the appropriate team while the conversation is still recent. The follow-up begins with context. Colleagues know what was discussed and can help move it forward. A customer benefits from the relationship without having to start the conversation over with each new person.

Then look at intake. Purchase agreement terms arrive in a document, but they need to become information the production team can use. A connected workflow could extract those terms for a person to verify against the source agreement before transferring the approved information into production. That could reduce repeated entry and help carry consistent information into the next stage of the file.

For the employee, that could mean less time retyping details. For the customer asking about progress, connecting customer and order information could make it easier to provide a dependable answer.

Title review offers another useful example. An examiner identifies a commitment requirement. Connecting that finding to a trackable task in production, with examiner sign-off, could give the work a clear next step. The team could see what needs attention and track it through resolution.

These are the kinds of improvements worth getting excited about. They put better information within reach and help professionals spend more time serving customers and moving transactions forward.

Title professionals know that an answer is only useful if they can trust it. Connecting information should make its source easier to see and professional review easier to perform.

Legal description and survey checks are also areas to explore, including flagging potential discrepancies in property boundary measurements. Automation could help direct a professional’s attention to an issue that needs investigation, with qualified review determining its significance.

The same principle applies when an output affects a document or recorded instrument. Keep the source visible, establish the appropriate review and record the final decision. AI can help organize information and flag issues, while qualified professionals remain responsible for title-related judgments and approvals. In title, accuracy is the product.

Permissions belong in the workflow from the beginning, too. Decide what a tool can access, which actions it can take and when human review or approval is required. Log its actions so the team can understand how a result was reached. Those decisions help make connected workflows dependable enough for people to use with confidence.

For leaders deciding where to begin, I would start by following a single file through its handoffs. Where do people re-enter information? Where does a finding wait for someone to assign the next action? Which customer questions take several conversations to answer?

Choose one connection to improve, then measure the difference. Look at repeated entry, response times and whether customers receive clearer answers. Let those results guide the next step.

We have experienced professionals, valuable information and people already willing to work with AI. Bringing those strengths together can help make each handoff more useful and each customer conversation more informed. That is progress customers will feel. And that is worth building.

Ryan Ozonian is the Senior Director of Innovation & AI at Williston Financial Group.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5573. Why homebuilders need business plans that test scenarios

Scott Cox explains why forcing long-range plans to match annual budgets shifts focus to deadlines over analysis. He recommends a 1-page output and a scenario-ready model leaders can adjust without analyst help.  AI Summary

[In the fourth of seven excerpts from ‘Less Wrong, More Right,’ Scott Cox argues argues a 5-year business plan should be a thinking tool, not a control document. He shares two tests: keep key output to one page and use a single assumptions page for scenario changes.]

Sometimes I think the most misunderstood part of our business is the business plan.

The real purpose is to learn about your business and understand the consequences of the choices available to you. If we go in this direction, what does it mean for our capitalization and our risk? How many people will we need, and when? Is our subcontractor base capable of that volume? For this to pay off, how long does the market have to hold? A plan exists to force that thinking. Everything else it does — satisfying the bank, setting the bonus targets, giving the board something to approve — is a byproduct, and the byproducts have a way of eating the main course.

I sat in a business plan meeting for the division of a multi-region builder. A number of organizational things were in flux, the market was slipping, and to be fair to the local team, they were being asked to work on too many initiatives at once. While everyone debated next year’s goals, I was looking at year five. I did a simple return-on-assets calculation on the page in front of me. It was terrible. I asked whether that was really what they expected, because if that was the plan, I could not support doing any new deals at all. The return on capital did not justify the investment.

After what I will politely describe as an agitated discussion, we got down to the why — the size of the deals, the type of deals, the organizational structure, the capital those choices required. And that should have become the start of a worthwhile conversation. Next year’s results were, within limits, going to be what they were going to be. The bigger issues were the ones worth the room’s time.

Then the deadline arrived. Divisional plans had to be consolidated. The banks and others were waiting. Some minor tweaks were made and the plan went out substantially as drafted. I doubt anyone looked past year one in that document ever again.

That is the failure I want to dwell on, because it was not a failure of intelligence or effort. It was a process that answered to form and deadline instead of thought — a date to hit, a box to check — and once those became the real assignment, the thinking we’d just started in that room stopped mattering.

What we should have been able to do, right there, was stop the meeting and start putting different approaches into the model. Bigger deals, fewer of them. Entitled land versus unentitled. Different timing. Then look at what came out — capital required, when it came back, what the returns actually were. We could not, so we did not. The model was capable of producing one future in enormous detail and incapable of producing a second one at all.

Underneath all of this is an instinct I want to focus on, because it is the one doing the damage. People believe everything should foot. The five-year plan should tie to the annual budget, which should tie to the phase budgets, which should tie to the cash flow. It feels like discipline. It is not.

Budgets are control instruments. Plans are thinking instruments. A control instrument has to foot — that is its job. A six-month cash flow projection cannot be materially wrong without serious consequences. An annual budget is an accountability document and people are going to be held to it. A phase budget for a project you are about to start is a commitment on money you are about to spend. All of those demand precision.

A five-year company plan does not. It is for asking what happens if we run this business differently? When you force a thinking instrument to reconcile with a control instrument, the thinking instrument always loses — because the deadline always belongs to the control instrument. That is not a hypothetical. That is exactly what happened in the meeting I just described.

The first is the one-page test, and it is a test of the output. If what you circulate, at least the important parts, does not fit on an 11×17, you have included things that do not matter. That is partly a communication discipline — that is how a lot of people are actually going to read it — but it is mostly a forcing function. Something has to be left off, and deciding what gets left off is the same as deciding what matters.

The second is a test of the design of the model, and it is the one I care about more. Can the CEO change the assumptions herself, in the room, in real time, to test an idea — without the analyst who built the model sitting next to her? Can I take it home, pour a bourbon after dinner, and try three scenarios on my own? If the answer is yes, the model is simple enough. If the answer is no, you do not have a tool. You have a document.

Back-up tabs are fine. Detail underneath is fine. The requirement is that a single, clearly marked assumptions page drives all of it with comprehensible results, and that changing one thing changes everything downstream without anyone opening the hood.

The principle underneath is that granularity should be set by what you need to move, not by what the budget happens to contain.

The 11×17 should just be a bigger, prettier version of the yellow pad. If it is anything more than that, ask yourself what all the rest of it is actually for.

Adapted from Less Wrong, More Right (Part III: Running the Business), available on Amazon.

#5572. Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Predicts ‘Will Crypto Recover in November’

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading near $75,800–$76,000 and Ethereum (ETH) is around $2,230–$2,235 as of November 8, 2026. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts, ‘Will crypto recover in November? ‘, which is the question on many traders’ lips heading into a big week across the markets.

Bitcoin sits roughly 40% below its October 2025 peak of about $126,000, while Ethereum remains well off its own highs. The market is asking whether crypto can stage a meaningful recovery this month. After the post-midterm bounce, both assets have consolidated.

Bitcoin has held the mid-$70,000s after testing higher levels earlier in the recovery, while Ethereum continues to lag, trading with a relatively weak ETH/BTC ratio near 0.0295.

This is typical in the early stages of a potential recovery, when Bitcoin usually leads, which is why all eyes should be on BTC USD over the coming week.

Bitcoin has formed a series of higher lows since the mid-year troughs and is defending the $74,800–$75,500 zone. A weekly close back above $81,000–$82,000 would strengthen the case for a durable base.

A break below $74,000 would reopen downside risk toward the low $70,000s. Ethereum remains softer. It is struggling to reclaim key moving averages and needs a sustained move through $2,400–$2,500 to show relative strength returning.

Until the ETH/BTC ratio turns higher, a full “altcoin season” style recovery remains unlikely, but a shift in market conditions can quickly change sentiment.

CRYPTO THIS WEEKNovember 9–15, 2026A busy week across crypto markets, policy, institutions and blockchain infrastructure. Inflation, exchange and ecosystem updates will shape the week.THE HIGHLIGHTS:✧ China October inflation data arrives November 9.✧ US CPI is out… pic.twitter.com/26z29H08Aa

The most immediate event is the October CPI report on Tuesday, November 10. Consensus expects a cooling in the monthly rate (around +0.2–0.3% headline). A softer-than-expected print would ease rate-hike fears, support risk assets, and give Bitcoin and Ethereum room to push higher into the second half of the month.

A hotter reading would reinforce the “higher-for-longer” narrative, pressure yields higher, and likely stall or reverse the recent rebound.

Soft inflation and resilient but not overheating growth data would be constructive. Sticky inflation or stronger-than-expected economic prints that raise December rate-hike odds would act as a headwind. Spot Bitcoin ETF flows remain the marginal driver.

Recent weekly outflows have weighed on price, so a return to consistent net inflows would be an important confirmation of recovering institutional demand.

Stablecoin growth and on-chain activity continue to favor Ethereum over the longer term, but near-term price action is still dominated by macro and Bitcoin leadership.

A modest recovery is possible if the November 10 CPI comes in soft and ETF flows stabilize. In that scenario, Bitcoin could retest the $82,000–$85,000 area and Ethereum could push back toward $2,400–$2,500 by month-end.

A hotter inflation print or continued ETF outflows would likely keep the market range-bound or push prices back toward recent lows. A full-blown bull-market breakout to new all-time highs is unlikely in November.

The more realistic path is a grinding recovery that builds through the end of 2026 and into 2027, assuming inflation continues to cool and institutional demand returns.

For now, the November CPI print is the single most important near-term catalyst that will decide whether the post-midterm bounce has legs or fades.

#5571. CTM Research Finds One in Five Adults Say They Tried to Contact a Mental Health Provider and Never Heard Back

New research examines persistent barriers to behavioral health care, generational differences in AI adoption, and the importance of human connection

ODENTON, Md. and MILLERSVILLE, Md., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- One in five U.S. adults who tried to contact a mental health or addiction treatment provider reported they never received a response, according to CTM's second annual behavioral health survey. The findings reveal persistent challenges in accessing care and explore how consumers' attitudes toward artificial intelligence are shaping the way they seek behavioral health support.

The findings come amid ongoing challenges in the behavioral health system and growing interest in AI as a tool for navigating care. According to the Health Resources and Services Administration, 137 million Americans live in a mental health professional shortage area, underscoring the challenges many communities face in accessing care.

CTM's research suggests that while people are exploring new options, getting connected to a person who can help remains central to the care journey. Three-quarters of respondents said they are comfortable speaking with a live person by phone about a mental health or addiction concern, up from 64% in 2025. Yet one in five respondents said they had tried to contact a mental health or addiction treatment provider and never heard back, a figure unchanged from last year.

"When someone reaches out for help, they shouldn't have to wonder whether anyone will respond," said Todd Fisher, co-founder and CEO of CTM. "In behavioral healthcare, technology should help providers connect with people more quickly and consistently, not create another hurdle. Whether reaching out by phone, text, or another channel, the goal is to help them reach trusted care that can understand their situation and guide them toward support."

The data underscores an opportunity for behavioral health providers to make the path to care more accessible by offering multiple ways to connect, improving follow-up, and using technology to support the people responsible for helping patients. As AI becomes more embedded into how patients find health information, providers must consider not only which tools they adopt, but how those tools help people move from an initial question to meaningful support.

The full report, The Changing Face of Mental Health Access, explores these findings and their implications for behavioral health providers navigating evolving consumer expectations. To access the report, visit https://tinyurl.com/3pyys555.

CTM commissioned kNOW Instant Insights to survey 1,000 U.S. adults ages 18 and older from August 31 to September 3, 2026. Year-over-year comparisons are included where survey questions and response options were consistent.

#5570. PitchBook opens its platform to startups for free and debuts Origin deal sourcing service

Private markets data provider PitchBook Data Inc. today opened its platform to startups for free at Web Summit in Lisbon.

Those that sign up have to share their financials. Some of that information will reach investors through the company’s new deal sourcing service, PitchBook Origin.

The launches come as more startups than ever are landing a first round. In the U.S., the 2021 record for first-time financings had already fallen by the end of September, PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association found in their latest Venture Monitor report.

PitchBook credits artificial intelligence with part of that growth, since the technology has made companies easier to start. AI tools have also compressed investor diligence from weeks to days. Sourcing has not kept pace, the company argues, particularly where the signals are not public.

Free access for startups runs through a program called PitchBook for Startups. Founders who have bootstrapped or raised only from angels, grants or accelerators qualify as long as they are now seeking a first institutional round and can show at least a mockup of their product.

Once a startup has handed over its financials and details on its leadership team and product, its founders can use the PitchBook platform to research which firms are actively writing checks in their sector and stage. Investor research tops PitchBook’s own list of what founders can do with the access.

That founder data lands in a much bigger pool on the Origin side, where coverage starts at about 25 million companies and 250 million people profiles. Bootstrapped businesses and companies that have not yet raised money or announced what they are building are part of that count, and some 15 million of the companies are new to PitchBook.

Third-party data enrichment and PitchBook’s own machine learning models supply part of the coverage. PitchBook said it has not had founder-verified data at scale before.

Each company gets a score, and investors can tune relevance filters to their own criteria. Real-time alerts, saved searches and customer relationship management integrations are meant to replace the manual monitoring that deal teams do now.

Chief Solutions Officer Paul Santarelli said the missing piece for investors has been visibility into “the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see.” Every company that joins the startup program and contributes verified information sharpens that picture, he said.

PitchBook “was once a startup itself, working to get in front of the right backers,” President and Chief Operating Officer Rod Diefendorf said. Founded in 2007, the Seattle company now serves more than 100,000 clients worldwide. Morningstar Inc. has owned it since 2016.

Startups can apply for the program now. Origin is available as a standalone product or as an add-on to the main PitchBook platform.

#5569. Asset Based Lending closes $200M securitization

Asset Based Lending closed its largest deal, a $200M unrated securitization backed by business-purpose residential loans. ABL 2026 RTL-1 allows up to 65% ground-up infill construction collateral and brings cumulative securitization volume to $723M.  AI Summary

Asset Based Lending (ABL), a private real estate lender, announced on Tuesday that it closed a $200 million securitization, its largest to date, backed by business-purpose residential real estate loans, including a significant concentration of ground-up construction loans.

The transaction, ABL 2026 RTL-1, priced Oct. 15 and closed Oct. 26. It marks the company’s fourth unrated securitization and brings its cumulative securitization volume to $723 million.

Up to 65% of the collateral pool is eligible to consist of ground-up infill construction loans, a segment that has been central to ABL’s lending strategy since 2014.

The transaction came amid volatility in the securitization market and increased investor scrutiny of credit risk, said Daniel Gotay, ABL’s head of capital markets. Despite these conditions, the company secured what he described as some of the tightest pricing levels for an unrated issuer.

“What is most exciting about this one is that we’re not just doing our fourth, but that the market was a tricky market this time around,” Gotay said in an interview with HousingWire. “For us to execute at one of the sharpest levels for an unrated issuer, and to do that with the highest concentration of ground-up construction, really spoke to the presence that we’ve worked hard to build on Wall Street.”

Gotay said investors were particularly focused on how lenders would manage credit and construction risks over the next two years. ABL completed more than 20 virtual investor meetings ahead of the transaction, highlighting its underwriting and servicing practices.

The company services its loans in-house and uses a high-touch approach to managing projects, Gotay said. He added that investors also evaluated ABL’s broader portfolio, which has maintained a weighted average credit score of 740 and a weighted average loan-to-value ratio of 64%.

ABL has kept its weighted average LTV in the low 60% range for much of the past decade, Gotay said, contrasting that with some competing securitizations featuring LTV ratios in the upper-60% to low-70% range.

Investor appetite for the asset class remains strong despite heightened caution, Gotay said. International capital, including funds based in the United Kingdom and Japan, is increasingly looking to invest in U.S. asset-backed securities. “Even though they’re a little more on guard because of what’s happening, they still have to deploy their money for this type of asset,” he said.

Kevin Rodman, CEO of Asset Based Lending, said the transaction reflects the company’s experience in financing residential construction.

“We are proud to lead the industry in financing ground-up construction, and to do it at a cost that keeps our pricing competitive for the builders we serve,” Rodman said in a statement. “This transaction underscores the strength of the platform our team has built and the confidence investors have in our credit. Every one of these loans puts new housing on the ground.”

Gotay said ground-up construction has long been a core part of ABL’s business and will remain a significant share of its lending activity.

“The firm is really built to manufacture and manage infill ground-up construction since, really, 2014,” he said. “That’s been our specialty in the market and where we win the most deals.”

Performance Trust Capital Partners served as structuring agent, while Nomura Securities International and Mizuho Securities USA served as joint bookrunners.

The securitization also reflects ABL’s expanding geographic footprint, with collateral spanning the Northeast, Sun Belt, Rust Belt and South. The company said it plans to grow beyond its established Northeast presence and finance residential development in additional markets across the country.

#5566. AI security startup Bay launches with $50M to vet agent actions before they run

Israeli artificial intelligence security startup Bay AI Inc. launched today with $50 million in funding to let enterprises vet each action an AI agent tries to take before it runs.

Bay provides software that tracks the agents working across a company, whether they sit on an employee’s laptop, inside a cloud workload or in a software-as-a-service application. One set of policies covers them all.

First-generation AI security tools mostly filter prompts and responses. Bay argues that misses where the damage happens, since a harmless-looking prompt can still end with an agent deleting a production database.

The founders ran into that kind of failure themselves when one of their own coding agents, working with its normal permissions, tried to expose a cloud environment to the internet to finish a test. They still have the screenshot.

Bay installs through the mobile device management or endpoint detection and response tools a customer already has, and the company says it takes under five minutes. A scanner called Wave inventories the agents, extensions and local models on each machine and leaves nothing running once it finishes.

Each time an agent proposes an action, the AI tool running it hands the request to Bay Enforcer, a static binary, through a native hook. The check happens on the machine itself with the whole session as context, and Bay said a verdict comes back in milliseconds, sometimes as a prompt asking the user to approve the step. Anything judged too risky never runs.

The policy behind those verdicts comes from Bay’s Lighthouse system, which drafts a separate one for each team from the last 30 days of agent activity, so security staff are not writing rules every time someone picks up a new tool. Teams can test a policy against the previous month first and see what it would have stopped. Bay said false positives run under 1%.

Security leaders are often handed an enterprise-wide AI rollout with a year-end deadline, co-founder and Chief Executive Yuval Zacharia said, or find that agents have already spread across the company and “it’s the Wild West.” She wants security to become “the reason AI ships faster, not the reason it stalls.”

Micron Technology Inc., Wix.com Ltd., ClickUp Inc. and Peloton Interactive Inc. are among the dozens of enterprise customers signed in the nine months since Bay was founded. Fortune 100 companies on the platform tripled their use of autonomous agents in just under 30 days, the company said.

Zacharia founded Bay with Chief Product Officer Aner Morag and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich. The three knew each other from the Israel Defense Forces’ Unit 8200, where Zacharia led a department of about 50 people before becoming the first intelligence officer there to cross into offensive cyber operations. After the military she ran security research and AI at Cyber Hunters Ltd.

Danilovich was an early employee at Preempt Security Inc. and stayed six years at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. after it bought the startup in 2020. Most of Bay’s research team followed him over. Morag was the first employee at Noname Security.

The $50 million comes from two rounds. Battery Ventures LP led the larger $37 million Series A round, and Micron’s venture arm, Micron Ventures, also participated after the chipmaker started out as a Bay customer. Wiz Inc. Chief Executive Assaf Rappaport put in money personally. The remaining $13 million came from a previously undisclosed seed round co-led by YL Ventures Ltd. and Striker Venture Partners.

Yoav Leitersdorf, managing partner at YL Ventures, said his firm looked at a crowded field of AI endpoint security companies before picking Bay. He believes it can become “as fundamental to enterprise AI adoption as the network firewall was to the internet era.”

Engineering and product hiring will continue in Tel Aviv, where Bay is based, with the sales, marketing and customer teams growing in the U.S. and Europe. Enterprises can buy the platform now.

#5564. Vodacom will seek partners to build AI data centers across Africa

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CEO Shameel Joosub names Egypt, Kenya and South Africa as bigger markets; half-year headline earnings rose 25.6%

Vodacom Group will seek partners for the construction of AI data centers across Africa, splitting the costs and drawing on outside know-how, CEO Shameel Joosub told Bloomberg. The Johannesburg-based company, majority-owned by Vodafone Group, made the comments as it reported half-year results.

Vodacom is co-investing with Elsewedy Electric and Cassava Technologies in an AI data center in Egypt, the company said in its results presentation. Joosub said in the interview that Vodacom will look at other markets, including South Africa and Kenya.

"Egypt, Kenya, South Africa are our bigger markets," Joosub said, according to Bloomberg. "It will be a big investment, and that is why we're bringing on partners."

The data centers, held in joint ventures, will draw their funding from both equity and debt, Joosub said. Vodacom will hold a stake in the facilities and probably handle most of the sales to customers, he said.

For the six months ended Sept. 30, Vodacom’s headline earnings attributable to equity holders rose 25.6% to R11.3 billion (about $646 million). Headline earnings per share rose 25.7% to 587 cents. Dividend per share rose 7.6% to 355 cents, and customers grew 11.8% to 250 million.

Service revenue rose 29.4% to R85.1 billion (about $4.9 billion), and EBITDA rose 40.0% to R42.7 billion (about $2.4 billion). Reported growth rates reflect the consolidation of Safaricom from the second quarter, the company said. On a pro-forma basis, service revenue rose 13.3% and EBITDA rose 18.0%.

Vodacom's stake in Safaricom rose to 55% from 35% effective June 30, 2026, and the transaction remains subject to appeal, the company said.

Africa represents under 1% of data-center capacity, while South Africa is home to most of the computing power on the continent, according to Bloomberg. Rival MTN Group has teamed up with an investment platform based in the Middle East to begin work on AI data centers in both Nigeria and South Africa.

Vodacom stock gained close to 5% in Tuesday trading on the Johannesburg exchange.

#5562. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.
