#5513. Justice Department is suing Lyft for $53 million over alleged disability discrimination

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The lawsuit alleges Lyft and its drivers refuse rides to passengers with service dogs and stowable wheelchairs

On Monday, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against Lyft $LYFT, accusing the ride-hailing company of discrimination toward riders with disabilities, among them people traveling with service animals and stowable wheelchairs.

The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, seeks $53 million on behalf of people with disabilities who lodged complaints with Lyft or the department, the department said. The department is demanding that Lyft pay a civil penalty as well.

The department contends that Lyft broke Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, a provision that prohibits private transportation companies from discriminating on the basis of disability. The complaint says Lyft and its drivers turn away passengers who have disabilities and then bill cancellation fees to riders who were denied rides. It also says Lyft declines to modify its policies where needed, including by denying riders with mobility disabilities the option to sit in the front seat.

The department wants a court order compelling Lyft to halt the alleged conduct, bring its policies into line with the ADA and provide legal instruction to employees and drivers.

"Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on rideshare services free of discrimination," Acting Assistant Attorney General Jesus A. Osete of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division said in a statement. "We intend to uphold the ADA's promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services."

U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California pointed to the government's case against Uber $UBER. "We take these allegations of misconduct seriously and, like our case against Uber for similar discriminatory conduct, we will devote all the resources necessary to make things right," Missakian said in a statement.

Lyft disagrees with the allegations, according to Reuters. "We have long-standing policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation," the company said in a statement, according to Reuters. Lyft said it cooperated with the Justice Department during its review.

The government sued Uber last year under the same federal law, seeking $125 million for people subjected to alleged discrimination who had complained to Uber or the Justice Department, according to Reuters. Uber rejected every one of the accusations.

#5512. Tech Moves: Microsoft loses a CVP to AWS and gains one from Alteryx; Lila Bio and BECU name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 3, 2026 at 2:30 pm

— After more than 33 years at Microsoft, Mazhar Mohammed has left to become vice president of AWS Streaming and Messaging at Amazon.

Mohammed joined Microsoft as a software design engineer on Windows NT straight out of a master’s degree program. Over the decades, he also worked on messaging, mobile services and partner experience for cloud services. He most recently served as corporate VP for the commerce and fraud protection platform.

His LinkedIn post was short and to the point. Mohammed said he was “happy to share” the news, and the post featured a photo of an Amazon box with the message “Alexa, play ‘New Beginnings.’”

— Microsoft has named Chad Thompson as CVP of Agent Cloud, a group within the company developing technology that allows businesses to deploy AI agents and put them to work across their organizations.

“My view: enterprise is where AI pays off. Not in demos, but in measurable results. Lower costs, faster cycle times, better decisions, and work that gets done without someone pushing it along,” Thompson wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Thompson joins from Alteryx. He previously spent six years at Amazon, departing as general manager of Amazon Glow. Other past employers include Smartsheet, Exasol and Adobe.

— Gail Carpenter has been named as VP and chief financial officer of Global Entertainment and Advertising at Amazon. She was most recently CFO of Worldwide Stores Finance and has been with the company for 11 years.

— Seattle biotech startup Lila Bio has appointed Kimberly Ma as chief development officer. The company spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington and is using AI to design new proteins that can treat cancer with targeted radiation therapy. Last year it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop therapies for solid tumors.

Ma has 20 years of experience in oncology drug development, most recently as a leader at Abdera Therapeutics. She also worked at RayzeBio, where she led the clinical operations team and supported the company’s IPO and its $4.1 billion acquisition by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024.

— The not-for-profit credit union BECU has named Geoffrey Fonga as VP of AI transformation. The member-owned organization is based in Tukwila, Wash.

“For years, I helped organizations adopt and scale AI as an advisor and a vendor,” Fonga said. “Now I get to do the harder, more rewarding part: leading that transformation from the inside.”

Fonga joins from DataRobot. He previously held leadership roles at McKinsey & Company and Wells Fargo.

— Andre Woodson Jr. has taken a new role at Amazon as manager of U.S. state and local policy communications and external affairs. Woodson was previously a regional field communications manager and has been with the company for more than 12 years.

— Hanna Grene has left Microsoft, where she served as global go-to-market and innovation leader for energy, to join Xcel Energy. She will lead the company’s newly established Enterprise Growth and Commercialization group, effective Nov. 16.

— Seattle-based RevealDx,which is developing AI technology for detecting potentially cancerous lung nodules, has made two leadership appointments:

— Enterprise software company LogicGate has named two new leaders to the business, which is headquartered in Chicago and has multiple C-suite executives based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. Steve Smith has joined as managing director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Amanda Meglemre as general counsel.

— Former Cisco and Microsoft security executive Edna Conway was appointed to the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based tech company building accountability infrastructure for AI agents. Conway was with Cisco for 20 years before joining Microsoft in 2020 as VP and chief security and risk officer for Azure infrastructure.

— Avalanche Energy, a Seattle-based startup building fusion devices, has named Chris Riegel as head of talent acquisition. He joins from HiringKit, an HR company that Riegel co-founded. Former employers include Amazon and Unity Technologies.

In addition to chasing fusion, Avalanche is leading a team tackling DARPA’s nuclear battery challenge and launching FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies in Eastern Washington.

— Julie Averill, former chief information officer at lululemon and REI, has joined the UW Foundation Board, which helps raise philanthropic support for the university.

— Technology Alliance has appointed Jen Oleson, a senior director at Seattle-based consulting firm Slalom, to its board. Oleson will serve on the organization’s Research Capacity Committee.

— Ben Helsel has left Premera Blue Cross to join Kaiser Permanente, where he’ll serve as VP and general manager of commercial markets in Washington.

#5511. China's trade surplus topped $1 trillion for a second year, two months early

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Customs data showed a $1.04 trillion surplus through October, as imports rose 41.6% and exports 35.2% from a year earlier

China ran a trade surplus of $1.04 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026, topping $1 trillion for a second straight year with two months left, customs data showed on Tuesday.

The total stands against the $1.2 trillion record set across 2025, the year the surplus first went beyond $1 trillion. The 10-month figure is roughly 9% above where it stood a year earlier, according to Bloomberg.

October exports rose 35.2% from a year earlier, while imports climbed 41.6%. Analysts had expected a 32% rise in imports, according to CNBC. The October surplus came to $105.3 billion, the smallest since May, according to Bloomberg.

Chinese exports to the EU increased 24.4% in October, whereas purchases from the bloc fell by over 4%, which pushed the monthly surplus with the EU up to $33.4 billion. The year-to-date surplus with the bloc exceeds $310 billion, close to a third of the overall total, according to Bloomberg.

Exports to the U.S. were up 32.9% in October while imports from there increased by roughly 35%, producing a bilateral surplus of $32.7 billion.

Worldwide demand for artificial-intelligence equipment has underpinned Chinese shipments, according to CNBC. Chips and computer parts supply 40% of this year's rise in the value of exports compared with a year earlier, according to Bloomberg. Exports of high-tech goods rose 67% in October, the fastest pace since early 2021.

Imports of high-tech products were 72% higher by value in October, according to CNBC's calculations of official figures. China brought in just under 42 million tons of crude oil during the month, a level last topped in March, according to Bloomberg.

China's cumulative surplus stood at $938.11 billion through September, including a record monthly surplus of $133.5 billion that month.

China's Customs Tariff Commission said on Monday it would keep suspending a 24% additional tariff on U.S. imports for two months while retaining a 10% tariff. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in Shenzhen this month at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

#5509. Adnoc Gas doubled profit and raised its 2026 forecast as LNG exports recover

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Net income rose to $1.34 billion from $665 million in the second quarter, and guidance is now at least $4 billion

Adnoc Gas, a unit of Abu Dhabi National Oil Co., raised its full-year net income guidance on Tuesday, setting a floor of $4 billion, after its profit in the third quarter came in at twice the second-quarter level, the company said.

Net income reached $1.34 billion, up 101% from $665 million in the second quarter. EBITDA rose 70% from the prior quarter to $2.03 billion. Adnoc Gas had previously forecast full-year net income of $3.5 billion to $4 billion.

Sales within the UAE rose 20% from the second quarter, and domestic gas EBITDA climbed 28%. EBITDA from international product sales rose 106%, and sulfur EBITDA rose 249%.

Adnoc Gas shipped more liquefied natural gas across the Strait of Hormuz during the third quarter compared with the second, according to The Wall Street Journal. "It is a month-by-month improvement in the number of cargoes that are crossing the Strait of Hormuz," Chief Financial Officer Peter van Driel told The Wall Street Journal. Shipments have yet to climb back to what they were before the war, even with U.S. Navy ships escorting vessels, van Driel told The Wall Street Journal. Adnoc Gas's September exports were about 88% of 2025 levels.

The company said market conditions improved in the third quarter but that disruption to maritime movements through the strait continued to strain operations. It said its outlook depends on regional maritime conditions.

"Our operational strength and commercial agility enabled us to safely and reliably meet domestic and international demand and drive strong financial results despite continued challenging external conditions," Chief Executive Fatema Al Nuaimi said in a statement.

Al Nuaimi told The Wall Street Journal that Adnoc Gas has made no decision on projects to bypass the strait, including an LNG export facility at the Port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. "At this stage, there are no decisions made on any of these projects," she said.

The board approved a quarterly dividend of $940 million, up 5% from a year earlier and payable in December. Adnoc Gas said restoration of the damaged Habshan complex is on track to reach full capacity by the second quarter of 2027.

The U.S. struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz last week. Tehran has said the strait could reopen within two days if Washington meets seven demands, while the U.S. rejects Iran's claimed authority over the waterway. A U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding signed June 17 collapsed.

The strain on the waterway has pushed Abu Dhabi to expand its own gas production. In July, Adnoc approved a $6.2 billion investment in the Umm Shaif Gas Cap, which is expected to begin production by 2030.

#5508. Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

#5507. Why Is Crypto Down? Jensen Huang Chinese Spy Scandal Sends AI Stocks Into Chaos

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

We’re back to the same question again: Why is crypto down? Bitcoin and altcoins are taking another beating as Wall Street’s AI trade starts unraveling. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is now at the center of a growing Chinese espionage scandal. His alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset has put the world’s most valuable chipmaker under fresh scrutiny.

The timing could hardly be worse for investors. Technology stocks have already suffered a brutal selloff, with the Nasdaq entering correction territory. Nvidia shares plunged 9.3% during Thursday’s rout, while semiconductor stocks suffered their worst session in years.

NEW: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to cheating on his wife two days after a report dropped that U.S. intelligence believes he had a relationship with a Chinese spy."I was unfaithful to my wife," Huang said in a letter to Nvidia staff."My actions hurt her and our children.… pic.twitter.com/moB9B3nYlI

Now, an investigation into Huang’s personal and professional connections could introduce another shock. If confidence in Nvidia starts cracking, the consequences could extend well beyond the AI industry. Bitcoin and the wider crypto market are already feeling the pressure.

The latest crypto selloff follows a dramatic reversal across US technology markets. Bitcoin erased its post-election rally, falling below $75,000. Ethereum dropped more than 7%, while XRP and Solana also suffered heavy losses.

The Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.5% during the same session. The Nasdaq 100 lost 6.4%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index crashed 12%. Nvidia and AMD were among the biggest casualties.

This selloff has been DEVASTATING.The AI stocks have erased $13.2 TRILLION in market value from stocks’ 2026 highs.Only U.S and China have an annual GDP larger than that loss.Market value erased at six AI giants:– Alphabet: $1.62 trillion lost (−32%)– Nvidia: $1.49… pic.twitter.com/i065m2W4b4

More than $2.5 trillion in Nasdaq market cap disappeared during October. Investors are increasingly questioning if massive AI infrastructure investments will deliver sufficient returns. Major technology companies continue pouring billions into chips, data centers, and computing infrastructure.

Then add political uncertainty, which is adding another headache. Democrats secured control of both congressional chambers during the US midterm elections. Investors now fear greater opposition to data center expansion and potentially tougher regulatory scrutiny.

The resulting selloff has exposed how closely crypto trades with speculative technology investments. Bitcoin increasingly moves alongside high-growth equities when institutional investors adjust their risk exposure.

The damage has also spread into derivatives markets. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions disappeared during Thursday’s selloff. Most liquidations involved traders betting on higher prices.

That forced selling can quickly turn an ordinary correction into something considerably uglier. As Bitcoin falls, liquidations push prices lower and expose leveraged altcoin positions to further losses.

Nvidia’s problems have suddenly become considerably more personal. The company’s board announced an independent investigation yesterday. It wants to examine reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The controversy involves Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. US authorities reportedly suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

Megaspeed has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving access to advanced Nvidia chips restricted from export to China. Republican lawmakers have requested a briefing from Huang regarding the allegations.

Separately, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife. He apologized to his family and colleagues, accepting responsibility for his actions.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang sends a company-wide email regarding his recently reported relationship with a Chinese spy. pic.twitter.com/NTdoSgaxoy

The combination creates an uncomfortable situation for Nvidia shareholders. Huang is not simply another corporate executive. He remains the public face of the AI revolution and one of its most influential decision-makers.

A prolonged investigation could introduce uncertainty around Nvidia’s leadership, relationships with international customers, and exposure to geopolitical tensions.

Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. However, the investigation could keep the controversy alive while investors are already questioning AI valuations.

The biggest concern for crypto is what happens if the AI selloff spreads. Nvidia has become a central pillar of the global technology investment cycle. Its chips power the infrastructure behind many of the world’s largest AI projects.

If investors begin questioning the sustainability of that investment cycle, semiconductor stocks, data center operators, and technology companies could face another round of selling.

Bitcoin is particularly exposed because institutional investors increasingly treat it as part of their risk portfolios. When confidence disappears from technology markets, crypto often loses buyers alongside speculative equities.

The Binance security incident has added another source of pressure. The exchange’s clients withdrew approximately $6.1 billion following the exchange’s recent security breach.

That creates an uncomfortable combination of falling institutional confidence, weaker market liquidity, and leveraged positions being forced out. Bitcoin now needs a recovery in risk appetite to regain momentum. Otherwise, another wave of technology stock selling could drag crypto prices lower.

So why is crypto down? The AI market has a new problem to deal with, and Bitcoin is discovering that Nvidia’s troubles can become its troubles too.

#5505. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5503. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5502. Fed's Waller puts a half-point December rate hike on the table if inflation runs hot

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank ought to weigh a half-point interest rate increase at its December meeting if October consumer price data looks like the figures from the prior two months, according to Bloomberg.

Waller made the remarks Tuesday in a speech in London. "If, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points," he said, according to Bloomberg.

"In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting."

He said a quarter-point move in that scenario would damage the Fed's standing. "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," Waller said, according to Bloomberg.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to release the October consumer price index on Tuesday. The Fed's next policy meeting is Dec. 8-9. The 2-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed 4 basis points during Waller's remarks.

Swaps moved to fully price a quarter-point hike for December following Waller's remarks, versus odds of roughly 85% ahead of them, according to Bloomberg.

Questioned afterward by Bloomberg's Francine Lacqua, Waller said the Fed needs to act. "We are looking forward and saying we need to do something; at a minimum, probably take back the three insurance cuts that we put in last year," he told Bloomberg.

Waller said higher rates "will be needed, sooner rather than later," according to CNBC. He said carrying out the hikes matters more than their timing, and that "it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings."

The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% at its October meeting. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. The central bank raised rates by a quarter point in September, its first increase since July 2023.

Other officials had said after the October meeting that rates need to rise. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said "additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon." Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who votes on the December decision, said the Federal Open Market Committee "needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases."

#5501. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5500. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5499. Disney and Adobe are building custom generative AI models for parks and ESPN

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Adobe will give Disney early access to Firefly, Premiere and Photoshop under a multi-year alliance announced Monday

Walt Disney $DIS and Adobe $ADBE are building custom generative AI models for Disney’s theme parks, studios and ESPN under a multi-year alliance the companies announced on Monday at Adobe MAX in Miami Beach, Florida.

As an Official AI Innovation Partner of Disney, Adobe will provide early access to its AI, creative and media technologies, the company said. Those include Adobe Firefly, Adobe Firefly Foundry, Adobe Premiere and Adobe Photoshop, along with dedicated engineering and research resources for Disney's production pipeline.

Through Firefly Foundry, Disney will collaborate with Adobe on proprietary generative AI systems built around its own franchises and properties, Adobe said. The models learn from character attributes, environments and visual styles, which lets them produce output that is safe for commercial use and ready for production.

Walt Disney Imagineering Research & Development has used Firefly Foundry in theme park development, Adobe said. Its tools include a sketch-to-image model that takes artists' hand-drawn ideas and renders them as 2D concept art, plus a custom image model that produces assets faithful to the franchises.

The work will begin by shortening project schedules in Disney's Experiences division and supporting early concept work at StudioLAB, Walt Disney Studios' internal innovation arm, according to Reuters.

"We talk about the time frames in our projects in years — it's years' worth of development. And what Adobe Foundry has allowed us to do is compress the creative process that would have taken months to now being able to do that in hours and days," Kyle Laughlin, Disney's senior vice president of R&D technology and engineering, told Reuters.

Laughlin said the tools will help the team avoid expensive modifications on site after construction of park experiences gets under way. He said they are "in no way meant to replace" roles at Imagineering, according to Reuters.

Adobe joins StudioLAB as an Innovation Partner to explore internal creative workflows with Disney creatives and technologists, according to Adobe. At ESPN Edge, the sports network's innovation center, ESPN and Adobe will identify ways for AI to increase engagement with sports fans and to bring ESPN's archive to life.

The alliance also covers marketing activations, industry events and customer storytelling tied to Walt Disney World Resort, Disneyland Resort, Disney Cruise Line, ESPN Edge and StudioLAB. Adobe will increase its presence across Disney's media platforms. Co-innovation projects with StudioLAB and ESPN Edge are under way, and more activations will roll out over the alliance's term, Adobe said.

"Today's announcement marks the next chapter of the relationship," Hannah Elsakr, Adobe's vice president of GenAI New Business Ventures, said in a statement.

Becca Vodnoy, Disney's senior vice president of Corporate Alliances, said in a statement that the alliance gives Disney's creative teams "new ways to explore and develop their ideas."

#5498. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5497. Jensen Huang's affair aided at least $7.5 billion in AI chip shipments to China, report says

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia's board has launched an internal investigation, and the FBI is examining whether the CEO was targeted by foreign intelligence

Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing helped enable at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies, according to The Information, which cited two people who know her. Reuters said it could not independently verify the claims.

The businesswoman, Alice Huang, assembled a web of firms spanning China and Singapore, partnering with her sister and husband to obtain the chips, according to The Information. She is not related to Jensen Huang and is also known as Huang Le. When orders for chips caught up in U.S. export curbs stalled, she leaned on her connections at Nvidia and its distributors to lock in supply, according to The Information. That effort got roughly 240,000 chips, spanning H100, H200 and some A100 models, into China.

Shanghai Century Litong, a company based in China and founded in June 2023, sat at the hub of the network, according to The Information. By October 2023, it had been designated a preferred cloud partner by Nvidia, which put it first in line for the chips. Century Litong leased out computing capacity and ran data centers built on Nvidia chips, some of which are prohibited from being sold to China. A portion of the hardware ended up supporting Alibaba, Tencent and several smaller AI labs in China, according to The Information.

Alice Huang held a senior role at Megaspeed, a Singapore-registered company that U.S. authorities have investigated over the flow of Nvidia chips from Southeast Asia into China, according to The Information. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says it abides by all relevant regulations, according to Bloomberg. Nvidia has said before that its own review of Megaspeed turned up no sign of diversion.

Jensen Huang confirmed the affair on Sunday, and Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, according to Bloomberg. Nvidia said the probe followed reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The FBI is looking into whether Huang, 63, became the subject of a foreign intelligence operation, according to Reuters.

The New York Times reported that American officials received a briefing saying Alice Huang worked for China's Ministry of State Security, according to CNBC. China has rejected the allegation, calling it a smear. President Donald Trump said on Monday that Jensen Huang told him he "had no idea that she was a spy."

Jensen Huang has been asked to appear at a closed-door session before several House committees meeting jointly, to discuss Nvidia's security protocols. The session is scheduled for Nov. 18, according to Bloomberg.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren asked Huang in June to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about Nvidia's compliance with U.S. export control laws and its business in China.

#5496. Grand Theft Auto VI: the last pre-AI blockbuster video game of its kind

Ben Feder is the Managing Partner of TIRTA Ventures and the former CEO of Take-Two Interactive. He is a Trustee of the New York Academy of Art.

On November 19, millions of people, most of them men, will call in sick. They’ll descend into their basements, fire up their consoles and disappear into Rockstar Games’ fictional Vice City. TV news will cover it. Newspapers will write about it. Saturday Night Live will parody it. And Grand Theft Auto VI will likely generate more revenue than almost any entertainment property ever created.

The moment will be cultural, the experience epic, and the game, I expect, a masterpiece.

Not because Rockstar won’t make another great game (it will). Nor because AI will make today’s games faster and cheaper (it already has). GTA VI represents the culmination of a model of creativity that AI is about to upend.

For more than three decades, artistic ambition in narrative video games has been measured by scale. Bigger teams built bigger worlds. Larger budgets bought denser cities, longer scripts, more for players to do. The achievement was creative, technological and increasingly organizational. Rendering a virtual city is a technological challenge. Populating it with ten thousand hand-authored details, on schedule, across three continents, is a feat of creative coordination.

With GTA VI, Rockstar orchestrated thousands of artists, programmers, writers and designers, working for about a decade in pursuit of a single creative vision. While Take-Two has never disclosed what GTA VI cost to develop, public estimates range from $1 billion to $2 billion.

Creative work often requires deletion. Novelists cut chapters they love. Filmmakers leave their best scenes on the cutting-room floor. Late in the development of Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar cut roughly five hours of content from a game developed by some 1,600 people. Five hours is roughly the length of an entire Call of Duty campaign. That is the nature of the process. It has to be created before anyone can know it doesn’t belong.

The bigger the creative team, the harder it is to erase, rethink and begin again. In game development, every important creative decision sets hundreds, sometimes thousands, of writers, artists, engineers, animators and audio experts in motion. And when those pieces come together, the original idea may no longer work.

At that point, changing direction becomes a systems problem. Abandoning an idea can mean unwinding hundreds of interconnected decisions across disciplines, teams and production schedules. The later the change, the more expensive it becomes. Creative decisions become financial decisions.

AI lowers the cost of changing your mind.

Game developers have always prototyped, tested and discarded ideas. What AI changes is how far an idea can be developed before a studio commits the full weight of production behind it. If a small team can build something playable and expressive enough to assess earlier, the expensive decisions can come later, when there is a much better sense of what works. As the economics change, the creative process begins to invert: less about what can be made, more about what is worth keeping.

Painting faced a similar inflection point nearly two centuries ago. When photography arrived, many visual artists feared for their livelihoods, and some were right: the market for commissioned likenesses collapsed.

Yet others asked a different question: What will we create now? Freed from the need to represent reality faithfully, they created new, even radical, art forms: Impressionism, Cubism and abstraction.

Something similar is likely with games. Photography freed painters from the obligation to reproduce the visible world. AI can free game developers from much of the cost of changing course.

I suspect cultural historians will one day look back on GTA VI the way art historians look back on the last great realist painters: the fullest expression of one creative model just before the boundaries of the medium broke open to reveal entirely new forms.

The next masterpiece rarely looks like a bigger or cheaper version of the previous one. It looks like something no one thought to make before.

#5495. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Rocket Lab reported third-quarter results on Monday, with revenue of $267.8 million, up 73% from a year earlier, and a net loss of 12 cents a share.

Rocket Lab stock fell 6.6% in after-hours trading Monday to $54.97. Revenue topped the $255.71 million analysts expected, according to Benzinga. Analysts had forecast a loss of 6 cents a share.

The net loss was $79.7 million, compared with $18.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. The operating loss was $79.2 million, up from $59.0 million. The company recorded a $3.5 million income tax provision, versus a $41.1 million benefit a year earlier.

Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $18.0 million from $26.3 million. Operating cash flow was positive $7.2 million on a GAAP basis.

Backlog reached a record $3.57 billion, up 52% from the end of the second quarter, the company said. It signed about $1 billion in new launch contracts across its Electron, HASTE and Neutron rockets, plus $470 million for space systems. That brought the total launch backlog to 117 launches.

Neutron contracts from constellation operators totaled more than $515 million in the quarter, lifting that rocket's backlog to 16 missions. The company said the base launch price rose to $70 million for several of those missions. It said the maiden flight is slated for 2027 at the earliest.

For the fourth quarter, Rocket Lab expects revenue of $270 million to $290 million and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $14 million to $20 million. It guided to GAAP gross margins of 34% to 36%.

Rocket Lab had moved the target for Neutron's first launch to 2027 in an October filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company had planned for the reusable medium-lift rocket to debut in late 2025. In the filing, it said the shift came as the team continued development and added process improvements.

Rocket Lab also builds the Electron and HASTE small-lift rockets, which it describes as its current launch vehicles.

#5493. Jensen Huang is the AI boom’s key man. Now, that’s a problem

It’s just about the most relentless and pulpy headline imaginable: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, with a woman who’s an alleged Chinese spy no less.

The news bombshelled on Sunday, and the market reacted viscerally on Monday: Nvidia closed down 4.3%, with about $230 billion in shareholder value wiped out, as other tech companies like Google and Meta saw share price upticks (welcome after Thursday’s Nasdaq nightmare). And yes, the luridness certainly drew attention, as did the national security concerns now subject to investigation.

The underlying question of it all is simple: Where do Huang and Nvidia go from here? Huang is AI’s ultimate key man. But more importantly: Nvidia—indelibly associated with Huang—is AI’s arms dealer, controlling north of 80% of the global market for AI and data center GPUs.

So, Huang’s affair isn’t just a public markets story, it’s a private markets story, with many tendrils. For one, functionally every AI startup and LLM giant is dependent on Nvidia GPU clusters to train and run models. This, naturally, includes the biggest names, including OpenAI, Elon Musk’s xAI, and Anthropic (on the eve of its IPO, expected to be historically large).

Nvidia’s also widely, and I believe correctly, described as AI’s central bank. The company’s financial footprint is stamped across the AI-pilled private markets. Nvidia’s been a key investor in startups, including Ilya Sutskever’s Safe Superintelligence and robotics unicorn Figure AI, and in key neoclouds like Nebius—not to mention an acquirer, as was the case with Nvidia’s September $12.93 billion announced acquisition of open-source startup Hugging Face, which had its own host of venture backers, including Lux Capital and Salesforce. (Nvidia has also backed OpenAI and Anthropic, and at least 400 other startups, a look at PitchBook says.)

It goes even further: Nvidia’s existing partnerships across the private markets include deals with  Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to create $500 billion in financing opportunities for (you guessed it) compute and data centers.

It’s the ultimate “key man risk” story. I’ve never typed this sentence before, but it’s true: There are trillions at stake, and it all ties back to Huang, who decisively helped create the AI boom. And he’s now the reason the AI status quo is, at best, imperiled.

But Huang is also impossibly entrenched and vital, and there’s just too much financial infrastructure at stake. This story is still developing, as they say, and new revelations may yet come to light. But my guess: Whether it’s right or wrong, Huang survives this furor and remains CEO of Nvidia.

Starbucks $SBUX is launching a limited-edition Bearista Glass Cold Cup Surprise Box collection at select coffeehouses around the world on Tuesday, the company said. Each box holds one of five holiday-themed bear characters, and each cup costs $39.95 while supplies last.

#5491. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.
