#5490. Exclusive: Alterra Labs announces $12.5 million seed round to build training environments for medical AI

Alterra Labs, a New York startup building simulated medical environments to test and train AI models, is announcing a $12.5 million seed round led by Oak HC/FT, with participation from Flare Capital Partners and Company Ventures.

The company evaluates models on medical tasks to identify where they fail, then turns those failures into training exercises. Doctors and scientists help design the tasks and judge the models’ decisions, providing feedback developers can use to improve their systems.

In a simulated patient case, a model might be asked to decide which tests to order, with clinicians assessing whether its choices are medically appropriate.

Akash Kapoor, Alterra’s founder and CEO, told Fortune that today’s models can learn to operate the software while still struggling with the clinical judgment behind each action. “The models don’t know when not to do something for a patient, and how to deal with uncertainty,”  he said.

Stanford researchers found similar difficulties in PhysicianBench and HealthAdminBench, two benchmarks testing AI agents on clinical and administrative work. In each, the best-performing agent completed fewer than half of the tasks. Some agents described the correct action in a clinical note but never carried it out in the electronic health record. Others lost information as they moved between software systems.

Alterra turns clinicians’ assessments into scoring criteria and rewards used in reinforcement learning, which encourages models to repeat stronger decisions and avoid behaviors experts have flagged as unsafe. The company also builds environments for tasks involving medical imaging, clinical trials and telehealth.

Vig Chandramouli, the Oak HC/FT partner who led the investment, said Oak saw a pattern across the healthcare AI companies it has backed—adapting models for medical work took more than data. They also needed realistic environments and clinical judgment. AI labs are going through a similar shift, he said: “All of the money that went into ‘I need data’ is now evolving into ‘I need to understand how to successfully do work.’”

He sees an opportunity in building realistic simulations of the software clinicians and administrators use, such as electronic health records, insurer portals and billing systems, where AI models can practice real work. Frontier labs have yet to build deeply into those environments, he said. Creating realistic tasks within them requires people who understand both clinical work and model behavior.

“You can’t build this stuff without clinicians,” Chandramouli said. “And more specifically, clinicians who actually understand how AI works.”

Kapoor fits that profile. He studied machine learning before turning to medicine, pursued healthcare-focused machine learning research at the National Institutes of Health and completed three years at Columbia Medical School. Chandramouli said that “clinical backbone is essential” to making AI perform better in healthcare.

Kapoor started the company in 2025 while attending Columbia Medical School. Initially called ChartR, it worked with healthcare providers to study how frontier models behaved in clinical settings.

The models often appeared capable at first, Kapoor said. Their weaknesses became clearer when they had to follow a patient over time, consider large amounts of information or make a series of decisions. They also struggled to recognize when they lacked enough information to act safely. Those observations pushed the company toward working directly with model developers. Kapoor left medical school in his final year to work on Alterra full time.

Kapoor’s interest in healthcare safety began with his own experience as a patient. As a junior at UCLA, he said, he discovered a two-year-old X-ray report in his patient portal warning of a potentially cancerous tumor in his leg and recommending an immediate oncology referral. No one had told him about it. He was diagnosed with osteosarcoma, a rare bone cancer, and underwent surgery.

His work at Alterra now focuses on the judgments AI models struggle to make when patients do not fit textbook descriptions. Kapoor expects that work to require repeated testing and training as models gain capabilities and medical knowledge changes.

“It has a lot of knowledge,” he said. “It lacks a lot of judgment.”

Alterra says it works with several frontier labs, hospitals, medical societies and applied AI companies. According to Kapoor, frontier AI labs are its fastest-growing customer group, and the company earns revenue from training environments and post-training services.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5489. PepsiCo is cutting about 1,000 jobs in North America as sales lag

Free daily briefing on global business news.

PepsiCo's North America beverage volume fell 2% in the latest quarter, and the company cut its earnings outlook in October

PepsiCo $PEP is shedding roughly 1,000 positions in North America in an effort to fix a sales slump in the region, according to CNBC.

Ram Krishnan, CEO of PepsiCo North America, laid out the goals in a Monday memo to employees obtained by CNBC. "We need to be faster, more connected, and more capable, while continuing to invest in growth," Krishnan wrote.

The memo said "too much of how we work today remains complex and fragmented," according to Bloomberg. Krishnan told employees that PepsiCo will "make changes across parts of our organization" over the coming week, according to Bloomberg.

PepsiCo had roughly 306,000 employees globally at the end of last year, some 125,000 of them in the U.S., according to a company filing.

PepsiCo stock rose in afternoon trading on Monday. The stock is down less than 1% this year, while the S&P 500 is up more than 10%.

PepsiCo has also had trouble keeping its share of the salty snack market, according to Bloomberg, with shoppers being choosier about how they spend.

The company cut its full-year core earnings forecast last month. It now expects core earnings per share to grow 2.5% to 3.5% for fiscal 2026, down from prior guidance of growth at the low end of a 5% to 7% range.

North American beverage volume shrank 2% in the third quarter, while volume in the North American convenient foods division was flat. Chairman and CEO Ramon Laguarta said PepsiCo is pursuing structural cost reductions to finance growth-oriented investments.

PepsiCo cut prices on brands such as Lay's and Doritos by as much as 15% in February to win back consumers. Chief Financial Officer Steve Schmitt said on the company's earnings call that the domestic turnaround is moving more slowly than expected.

#5488. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5487. Why top performers stall before the C-suite—and the shift that gets women there

Many high-performing women build careers by becoming trusted experts, exceptional operators and reliable problem-solvers. Those strengths are critical, but advancing to more senior leadership roles requires a shift: expanding your focus from leading a function to helping lead the entire enterprise.

One of the most effective ways to prepare women for executive and board-level leadership is to give them enterprise-level experiences before they’ve been promoted into senior leadership roles. At Thrivent, we talk about the importance of “wearing your enterprise hat.” The idea captures a leadership transition that matters more and more as leaders advance. Success requires understanding how decisions affect the broader organization and having the perspective to act accordingly.

That shift from “my team” to “the business” is one of the most important transitions a leader can make. And enterprise thinking can be developed with practice.

Successful functional leaders are often exceptional operators. They solve problems quickly, make sound decisions and consistently deliver results.

The challenge is that the behaviors that drive early-career success can become limiting at more senior levels. Leaders who remain at the center of the work may increase speed in the short term, but over time, that approach can restrict the capacity, decision-making and growth of others.

Wearing your enterprise hat starts with creating enough distance from the work to ask bigger questions:

Success is no longer measured only by what you personally accomplish. It is measured by the results you enable through others.

Enterprise thinking begins with curiosity.

Leaders who successfully make the leap to higher levels invest time in understanding the business beyond their area of expertise. They learn how decisions affect customers, financial performance, talent, risk, operations and long-term strategy.

That broader perspective helps leaders see connections that are not always visible from within a single function, division or department. It also allows them to contribute meaningfully to conversations that extend beyond their day-to-day responsibilities.

The most effective executives are not experts in everything. But they understand enough about the whole company to make informed decisions that advance shared goals—and they are humble enough to trust others’ expertise.

Enterprise thinking becomes most visible when resources are limited. Every leader can advocate for their team. The harder challenge is recognizing when the organization’s strategic direction requires prioritization, reallocation or a different course of action.

That may mean supporting a decision that benefits the broader organization, investing in a capability outside your area because it creates greater value overall, or saying “no” or “not now” to an initiative even when that decision creates short-term challenges for your own team.

These choices require leaders to look beyond functional optimization and focus on enterprise impact.

We cannot expect emerging leaders to demonstrate enterprise thinking if they’ve never had the opportunity to practice it.

One of senior leaders’ most essential responsibilities is creating experiences that expand perspectives. Cross-functional projects, enterprise-wide initiatives, strategic planning efforts and exposure to senior decision-making help future leaders understand how organizations operate beyond their immediate area of responsibility.

These opportunities are especially important for women who are preparing for executive and board-level roles. Experience builds credibility. It also builds the judgment and confidence required to lead through complexity.

Preparing the next generation of women leaders goes beyond identifying high-potential talent. It requires giving talented leaders opportunities to think, contribute and lead beyond the boundaries of their current roles.

By the time someone is being considered for the C-suite, enterprise thinking should already be how they operate. That leadership shift prepares executives not only to reach senior leadership but also to succeed once they get there.

The future belongs to leaders who can connect the dots across the enterprise, elevate those around them and make decisions that advance the whole organization. As businesses continually evolve, wearing your enterprise hat is more than an executive skill—it is a leadership imperative.

#5486. Google launches Gemini for Healthcare, and hospitals like Northwell hope it brings down your medical bill

Google Cloud says its newest AI product can help with one of Americans’ biggest complaints: the cost and redundancies of health care.

On Tuesday, the company launched Gemini for Healthcare, an AI product that connects to the records, billing and insurance systems that hospitals and insurers already use—and is able to act between those systems. Launch customers include Northwell Health, Highmark Health, HCA Healthcare, Optum, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, Hartford HealthCare and Stanford School of Medicine.

The new healthcare AI can pull a patient’s records from Epic and other systems into one single summary, flag gaps or conflicts between records, prepare and review prior authorizations, check what a patient’s insurance covers, estimate what they’ll owe, and search medical guidelines from groups like ASCO and the BMJ.

This comes as health costs keep climbing. Workers with employer coverage now pay $7,471 a year on average toward family premiums, up 9% from 2025, according to KFF’s annual employer survey released in October. When including what employers contribute, total family premiums rose 5% to $28,303, outpacing a 3.7% rise in wages and 2.7% inflation.

For the head of New York’s largest health system, part of that bill comes from records that don’t talk to each other.

“All the fragmentation of information in healthcare is what has led to, in my mind, some of the costs that have gotten away from us, and also overutilization,” John D’Angelo, who took over as CEO of Northwell in October 2025, told Fortune.

An emergency physician by training, he said he saw it in the ER. “I would treat people de novo, and the information is out there somewhere,” he said. “So I’m either playing detective or I just have to assume.” That could mean ordering a CT scan, he said, not knowing if they’ve had it four times already for the same condition.

When you walk into a doctor’s office, you inevitably are given a clipboard with papers you’re all but certain you’ve completed through the portal online. Then when you finally are whisked away to the doctor’s office, you’re asked the same questions you’re fairly certain were asked in the papers lining that very clipboard.

That constant asking and re-asking of questions leaves a poor taste in patients’ mouths, and that’s all before they were told to go “aaah.” Gemini for Healthcare is solving for that: it cites the source for each finding so clinicians can check it. For now, it can read patient records but not change them, so a doctor or nurse still makes any updates and decisions. In essence, it cuts down on the paperwork a doctor has to complete when they see a patient, bringing back that face-to-face consultation rather than letting paperwork pull doctors away from patients.

“Right now, for every 10 minutes a doctor spends with a patient, they’re 20 minutes on the computer documenting, capturing stuff, looking up the old data, tracking things down,” D’Angelo said.

Much of that time goes to insurers. Prior authorizations, the approvals insurers require before some treatments, are among the biggest burdens. Each physician completes about 40 prior authorizations a week, which takes around 13 hours of physician and staff time weekly, and 40% of practices have staff whose sole job is handling these requirements, according to the American Medical Association. The American Hospital Association estimates administrative costs make up 25% to 35% of U.S. health spending.

At Northwell, the fight with insurers takes a whole department. “I have like 400 employees whose sole job is fighting the insurance denials, and we overturn over 90% of them, but that’s a big labor cost,” D’Angelo said.

Karen Hanlon, president of Highmark Health, which owns both an insurer and the Allegheny Health Network hospitals, said doctors made clear what bothered them most. When Highmark asked its clinicians a few years ago what to fix after prior authorization, she said, “universally they said nothing else. Just keep focusing on prior authorization.”

Aashima Gupta, Google Cloud’s global director of healthcare strategy, said nurses and doctors now spend much of their day moving information between systems. “Humans are acting as an integration layer today,” she told Fortune. “They didn’t get into the profession to be glorified data-entry clerks. They want to be able to take care of the patients.”

Gemini for Healthcare launches with five ready-made “skills” — preset instructions for tasks like summarizing medical records, preparing for appointments and checking a patient’s insurance benefits — plus connectors to Epic, federal Medicare coverage data and medical guidelines from the American Society of Clinical Oncology and the BMJ.

In a demo with Fortune, Will Rosenfeld, Google Cloud’s healthcare data and AI lead, asked the system what was new in an outside specialist’s report that wasn’t in a patient’s Epic chart. In 35 seconds, it pulled the patient’s conditions, medications, allergies and labs, compared them with the outside report and flagged new lab results and an allergy the chart had missed, with each finding linked to its source. A clinician then decides whether to update the chart, since the system can read Epic records but not change them.

“A lot of the power of the product is just like simply one plus one equals three,” Rosenfeld told Fortune, describing how it puts a patient’s record next to coverage rules or medical research.

The same tool can answer cost questions during a visit. Gupta described a nurse asking whether a Medicare patient’s coverage pays for a skilled nursing facility, and what the copay would be, without making calls to find out. Rosenfeld said customers are especially interested in cost estimates. “It’s just something that’s really difficult for patients, to not know what their costs are going to look like,” he said.

Highmark already uses automation to cut waits. It says 78% of approved outpatient prior authorizations submitted digitally now go through automatically, so a patient can sometimes get approval before leaving the office. “They don’t have to take another day off work,” Hanlon told Fortune. She said a clinician reviews every case before Highmark issues a denial.

D’Angelo called automating the denial fights “part of driving the affordability conversation the right way,” and said Northwell runs on “a 1% margin business at best.” Money saved on paperwork, he said, could go to community health workers who keep patients out of the hospital.

He said faster records and notes could also shorten wait times without overworking doctors, letting offices “squeeze two more patients a day” in practices with long waits. “Not because I made them stay open later or I told the doctor, ‘Suck it up, miss lunch,’ but because they’re able to be more efficient,” he said.

“It shouldn’t replace the doctor or the nurse, but it should give the doctor or the nurse back to the patient,” he said.

Both D’Angelo and Hanlon said the potential savings come from catching illnesses earlier, with Gemini acting as a pseudo-preventative care measure, while also allowing people to gain trust within their medical professionals.

D’Angelo, for example, described a system that notices a former smoker turning 50, confirms insurance has approved lung cancer screening, and offers nearby appointments, all without having a human pour through the records in the first place.

“That’s how you also address affordability over the long term, as we get much further upstream on wellness and driving down chronic disease,” he said.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5485. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5484. Would You Take the Money? Microsoft Is Offering Employees Its Biggest Buyout Offer to Date.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The tech giant offered buyouts to a quarter of its workforce as it looks to reduce spending.

Two weeks ago, Microsoft presented 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce, with an enticing offer. They could choose to leave Microsoft of their own accord in exchange for a severance package.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” chief people officer Amy Coleman said in a memo to workers in late October.

According to a new report from The New York Times, Microsoft employees flocked to an internal website within an hour of the buyout announcement to find out if they had received an offer.

So many workers were checking at once that employees speculated that traffic had overwhelmed the site.

A handful of Microsoft employees who spoke with the Times said that the buyout offer added strain to an already tense relationship between employees and leadership. They said the buyout proposal arrived amid rising pressure to adopt AI, frustration over flat pay and deepening worries about job security.

The voluntary exit offer is the biggest in the company’s history and marks Microsoft’s second buyout this year.

For Microsoft employees, a buyout means weighing the options. Is the payment enough to make leaving worthwhile?

Workers look at the financial incentive offered by the buyout and weigh it against household expenses, health insurance costs and time needed to find another job. They usually take stock of their savings and consider if they are at risk of layoffs later.

If not enough people choose to accept the offer, Microsoft could resort to layoffs to cut costs. Buyouts are often “a precursor to layoffs,” Lindsay Witcher, a senior executive at career transition firm Randstad RiseSmart, said in an interview with CNBC in 2023.

A Microsoft spokesperson told Bloomberg that workers who accept this buyout offer will receive benefits similar to a regular severance package.

When Microsoft cut U.S. jobs earlier this year, its severance terms guaranteed at least 60 days of base pay. For most employees, the package topped out at 39 weeks of base pay, with the amount determined by their level and length of service, per Business Insider.

The spokesperson added that the buyout applies to employees on select teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K and India. Some employees on teams working on data centers, sales and marketing do not qualify for the buyout.

Eligible employees have until the first week of December to decide if they want to accept the buyout, according to GeekWire. Their departures are scheduled for the end of the year, per CNBC.

Microsoft told GeekWire that the buyout is not a sign that it needs fewer workers. Instead, the tech giant said the measure was one way it was adjusting to shifting business priorities.

Microsoft’s workforce numbered 223,000 people at the end of June, according to its annual filings. That headcount has been relatively flat since 2022, when the company started pouring more money into AI and data centers.

#5483. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5481. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5480. Customers Suing McDonald’s In Chicago Are Not Lovin’ the McRib

A federal judge says customers could reasonably expect a sandwich called the McRib to contain actual ribs.

The McRib may truly only be back for a limited time.

On Oct. 30, U.S. District Judge April M. Perry in Chicago ruled that a proposed class-action McRib lawsuit against McDonald’s can move forward. Filed by four consumers last December, the suit says the highly popular sandwich contains no rib meat. The plaintiffs allege the patty is made from cheaper pork parts like shoulder, heart and tripe and pressed into the shape of a rack of ribs.

The company describes the meat as “seasoned boneless pork,” according to The New York Times, and lists its ingredients on its website. It argued that the “Mc” prefix only marks the sandwich as a McDonald’s product and doesn’t promise rib meat. McDonald’s also denies using organ meat.

But Perry didn’t buy it. Sure, a McFlurry may not contain a literal flurry, but she found it reasonable for a customer to expect rib meat in something called the McRib. “The court is not persuaded by defendant’s many arguments that it would be unreasonable or fanciful to think the McRib contains rib meat,” she wrote. The suit seeks unspecified damages and an end to the McRib’s current marketing. Perry dismissed five claims but let the deception, fraud and unjust enrichment claims proceed.

#5479. Lumen CFO expects up to $1.5 billion from legacy copper amid pivot to AI connectivity

Good morning. As Lumen Technologies transforms from a legacy telecom company into an AI enterprise connectivity provider, it’s finding a new use for its old copper network: mining it.

“Copper is worth more to us mined than operated,” President and CFO Chris Stansbury said.

Lumen plans to turn off copper-based services in Iowa, Florida, Nevada and Utah, about 25% of its copper network, by the end of next year. At current copper prices, Lumen expects $1 billion to $1.5 billion in pretax net proceeds from copper recovery over the next five years, Stansbury said.

The benefits extend beyond the metal. Decommissioning will also cut the operating and capital costs of maintaining aging infrastructure, simplify operations, and free up resources for higher-return investments, he said.

“We’re now at the point in our transformation with legacy where the cash generation from revenue is actually not as good as what will be cash generation from mining the copper that’s in the ground,” Stansbury told me. “This industry is sitting on one of the largest copper mines in the world.”

Lumen plans to work with regulators and meet its service obligations as it stops marketing new copper services.

The strategy is part of a broader effort to reinvent Lumen, No. 354 on the Fortune 500, as an enterprise connectivity provider for the AI era. Lumen pairs its large fiber network with Alkira’s software, which works with any carrier. That lets companies connect and manage their data from one place, whether it sits on Lumen’s network, another provider’s network, in the cloud, or in data centers. The company recently announced three initiatives involving intelligent networking, AI energy challenges, quantum connectivity, and emerging security threats.

There are signs of progress. Lumen reported third-quarter revenue of $2.72 billion, down 12.1% year over year, largely reflecting the sale of its consumer fiber business to AT&T. But adjusted EBITDA reached $715 million, and its adjusted loss of 14 cents per share was narrower than analysts expected.

More importantly, strategic revenue, higher-growth enterprise and fiber-based services, rose 10% to $1.28 billion, driven by AI demand and private connectivity deals. Lumen reaffirmed its full-year EBITDA and free cash flow guidance.

The challenge will be sustaining that growth while replacing the revenue and cash of its legacy business.

CEO Kate Johnson and Stansbury have worked on the transformation for about four years. Johnson envisioned making Lumen’s network easier for businesses to consume.

“What Kate came in, and saw was the ability to effectively cloudify the network, just like the hyperscalers had done with compute and storage,” Stansbury said.

The effort has also required a cultural shift and change management.

“I think the approach that you take in having those conversations and making those tough decisions is treating people with respect and empathy, and being transparent—telling them what you can, when you can,” Stansbury said. He added: “I don’t want to say it makes those decisions easier, but I think it ultimately helps the organization transform from what was to what will be in a much better way.”

#5478. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

#5477. Your Next Customer Is an AI Agent. Here’s How to Market to It.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AEO and GEO are chapter one, but the next big shift is evolving further down the purchase funnel

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When most people hear “AI marketing,” they think of using AI to do marketing. This may mean writing copy faster, generating ad creative, automating outbound sequences, etc. That’s useful and has a huge impact on how marketers approach their jobs, but it’s not what I’m talking about.

I’m talking about marketing to AI. Specifically, to the agents that are starting to shop on behalf of people.

The first wave of AI search optimization (AEO, GEO, AIO, pick your acronym) was built around one shape of AI: the chatbot or answer engine. A shopper asks a question, an LLM writes an answer, and somewhere in that answer your brand shows up, or it doesn’t.

That framing got a lot right, but it is still largely rooted in how we think about traditional search, the only real difference being the shift from keywords to questions. That said, it has sparked a new discipline within marketing, one where many brands are tracking and investing energy in understanding how AI models read their site and content, which sources AI cites when answering brand-relevant questions, and how they stack up against competitors across LLM responses.

All of this is important, but just the tip of the iceberg. What marketers need to do next is evolve their GEO strategies to not only ensure their brand appears in the first answer, but also to ensure that as a shopper travels through the full buyer’s journey within the same AI search conversation, their products and services remain relevant and ultimately win the customer decision. The later portion of the journey used to happen after a shopper clicked from their initial Google search to your website. Now it lives entirely between the shopper and their agent.

This is where we’ve seen brands quietly lose. When my team ran 320 simulated shopper conversations, nearly three in ten brand mentions never turned into a recommendation. The brand showed up in the answer, and then somewhere further down the conversation the agent picked someone else. That lines up with independent research showing AI shopping assistants get worse as conversations get longer. Getting mentioned and getting picked are two different things, and right now most brands are only measuring the first one.

It is important to note that not all agents look like chatbots, and as AI Search evolves into new formats, so must our marketing strategies.

Look at Meta’s Muse. It launched on Sept. 8 and quickly climbed to the top of the App Store. It’s not really a chatbot; it’s a personal agent that runs on its own cloud machine, opens its own browser, scans retail sites, compares prices, and checks out for you. It keeps a shopping profile on each person, tracking their actions and tastes.

And Muse is one example, but there are agents that live in text messages, inside browsers, in glasses, and in voice. Many brands and retailers are building their own agentic shopping experience too. Each iteration and version finds products differently, reads them differently, and ultimately guides their users down buyer journeys in different ways. These are all new potential blind spots that we, as marketers, must learn to address and influence to reach our shoppers via their agent.

They pull from everywhere. In one early test, most of Muse’s product picks came from live websites rather than Meta’s own catalog, even though the catalog offered far more options. Your site, your feeds and every catalog you’re listed in all count.

They act, not just answer. An agent that can check out has to get through your site first. Amazon has already blocked Muse. Plenty of brands are blocking agents without knowing it, through bot protection built for a world where bots were the threat.

They remember. A profile that says “Wide feet, and need extra support for bad knees” shapes every future recommendation. That’s potential brand loyalty, written down by a machine.

They report to a human. Muse asks for approval before it makes a purchase. The agent has to justify its pick and give its reasons.

That last point matters more than most brands realize, and it’s a big part of where that three-in-ten number comes from. Agents don’t just find you, they do a lot of the “choosing” on behalf of their shopper. In our simulations, in which shoppers were looking for headphones under $150, the shift from mentioning a brand to recommending it occurred once the shopper provided a budget. One premium brand was mentioned in 82 answers and recommended in none. Another got named as a premium option and then dropped as soon as the price cap came up, losing the chance to sell premium value to justify a higher cost.

Meanwhile, a value brand went from never being recommended when budget came up to almost always being recommended afterward, which is a price-fit story, not a trust story. The brands that dropped off weren’t unknown to the agent, they just didn’t fit the shopper’s constraints, which meant the agent had nothing to justify the pick with when it came time to choose.

Here’s the issue with AEO and GEO as labels: they name the interface.

A lot of people, Forrester included, are now saying the agent is your new customer. I don’t think that’s quite right. The customer hasn’t changed; the person is still the one you’re trying to win, but more and more they’re represented by an agent that does the buying for them, on a journey we aren’t used to. That agent is both a new gatekeeper and a new audience, and marketers need strategies for both.

So I think the more useful frame is marketing to agents. Not instead of GEO, but as an extension of. If GEO is how you show up when an agent answers, then marketing to agents more broadly is how you win. Being able to influence the entire AI assistant shopping journey is the target we need to keep in view. I think about this as “AI Search marketing” broadly.

We’ve seen this before. “Internet marketing” eventually split into search, social, email, ecommerce, affiliate and a dozen other disciplines. Marketing to agents will split the same way. The brands that do well will be the ones that start treating the agent as a buyer worth winning now, not a bot to block, while the shapes are still settling.

You don’t need to rebuild anything this quarter. A few moves go a long way:

People still want the right product, at a fair price, from a brand they trust. What’s new is that more of the legwork goes to software that reads everything, never sees your homepage hero, and remembers how it went.

Market to the buyer, win the customer. Build for the whole job, not the initial chat response.

When most people hear “AI marketing,” they think of using AI to do marketing. This may mean writing copy faster, generating ad creative, automating outbound sequences, etc. That’s useful and has a huge impact on how marketers approach their jobs, but it’s not what I’m talking about.

I’m talking about marketing to AI. Specifically, to the agents that are starting to shop on behalf of people.

The first wave of AI search optimization (AEO, GEO, AIO, pick your acronym) was built around one shape of AI: the chatbot or answer engine. A shopper asks a question, an LLM writes an answer, and somewhere in that answer your brand shows up, or it doesn’t.

#5476. Exclusive: In the race for robot training data, ex-Meta researchers’ startup turns to gig workers with cameras

Memories.ai is paying people to show robots how to do their jobs. The San Francisco startup supplies first-person video data for robot training, with cameras capturing the hands-on details of preparing food, stocking shelves and repairing equipment.

The company is launching Memories Upload, a global gig-work platform where contributors take paid video-recording tasks to help train robots. Its wearable LUCI Pin camera, developed by Memories.ai, weighs under 45 grams and attaches magnetically to mounts worn on a person’s head, chest or wrist. It captures POV video of the contributors doing various tasks. Two cameras can be paired for stereo capture, providing views that help estimate depth.

Memories.ai says its network recorded more than 1 million hours of first-person video in the platform’s first month in beta and that it aims to collect more than 10 million hours by March 2027. The company was founded by former Meta researchers Shawn Shen and Ben Zhou. The company has raised $16 million in venture capital funding to date, including an $8 million seed round in July 2025 led by Susa Ventures, with investors including Samsung Next, and an $8 million “seed extension” in June this year.

Humanoid robotics startup Figure and Physical Intelligence, a startup that builds AI software “brains” that can control a variety of different types of robots and embodied AI devices, are both exploring how robots can learn from POV video footage. Figure’s Index platform pays people to record everyday tasks for its Helix AI models. Physical Intelligence has tested combining human video with teleoperation data, which is recorded as people control robots remotely, demonstrating how to complete tasks or handle unfamiliar objects and environments. Physical Intelligence co-founder Sergey Levine wrote in a blog post that human video and other supplementary data could provide “a source of knowledge about what can happen in the real world,” complementing data collected by robots themselves.

For a robot learning to make coffee, those recordings could show how someone grips a cup, positions it beneath a grinder and moves it without spilling. Footage from different kitchens, tools and ways of working can expose models to a wider variety of tasks and environments. Developers still work out how to translate those observed movements into actions suited to the robot’s own body.

“Recognizing an activity is different from understanding exactly how a hand grips a tool, moves an object or completes a step, especially when the camera is moving and objects are partly hidden,” Rick Zhuang, director of product and engineering for Cosmos at Nvidia, which works with Memories.ai, told Fortune.

Finding those details in a growing collection of footage is part of the problem Memories.ai is trying to solve. The company uses Nvidia’s Metropolis Video Search and Summarization tools to optimize video streaming and processing. Its video-captioning model is fine-tuned from Cosmos, Nvidia’s family of models for understanding the physical world, and it also uses Cosmos-based models to label actions. The company further trains Cosmos on curated video for customers’ specific tasks, a process known as post-training.

The resulting descriptions are tied to specific moments, letting developers search for an action and retrieve relevant examples without watching hours of recordings. “What stands out is the focus on making everyday human experience searchable and useful for robot learning,” Zhuang said of Memories.ai.

The company says its customers include three of the top five frontier AI labs, alongside robotics developers buying its first-person training data, although the company declined to name these customers citing non-disclosure agreements. Co-founder and CEO Shawn Shen told Fortune that customers increasingly want footage covering a wider range of work environments, tasks and camera angles. Two people making coffee in different kitchens can supply useful variation, he said, even when they are completing the same task. Developers also request wrist-level footage to see interactions that a camera on someone’s head might miss, such as exactly when a hand touches an object.

Adam Scraba, Nvidia’s head of physical AI ecosystem for vision agents, told Fortune that the wide variety of specialized tasks in heavy industry, coupled with the need for highly accurate models, presents one of the field’s hardest challenges.

“The training dataset for Vision AI and video analysis becomes critically important for basically all Physical AI solutions. Developers need to find the right corner-case examples, trust their labels and trace each annotation to the moment it describes,” he said.

Producing labels developers can trust is particularly difficult when hands make subtle movements, objects are partly hidden or the boundary between two actions is unclear, Zhuang said. Those cases make human review and evaluation essential. Human video is most useful alongside robot demonstrations and simulation, he added, helping developers connect observations of human work to actions a robot can perform.

Update, Nov. 10: This story has been updated to clarify the total amount of money Memories.ai has raised to date and to include information about the company’s June 2026 seed extension round.

#5475. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5474. AI Is Changing the Economics of SaaS Partnerships. Here’s How Founders Can Capitalize.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is reshaping the SaaS partner model, creating opportunities beyond traditional referral commissions and low-margin services.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A typical SaaS referral deal gives a partner 10-15% of first-year revenue, rarely enough to support sales, implementation and future growth. As SaaS made software easier to buy and deploy, much of the surrounding work became repeatable, pushing partners toward lower-margin services. Without a more profitable business to build around the platform, they will invest elsewhere.

AI gives partners something SaaS gradually took away: high-value work built on the platform, shaped by the customer’s context and sold as expertise rather than access. Not every AI engagement will be unique, nor should it be. The reusable parts like connectors, retrieval patterns, evaluation frameworks and managed operations will become more standard. But the decisions that make an AI system useful do not travel so easily from one customer to another. Which workflow should change? Which data can be used? Where does human review belong? What counts as a good answer, and who is accountable when it is wrong?

The building blocks may be familiar, but making the workflow safe, useful and adopted is not. It relies on industry judgment that the partner has built from years of being the person the client calls when something breaks.

This is not an argument that every partner should go train a model, or that every SaaS company should suddenly become a services business. Most customer deployments will be about workflow design, permitted data, integration, evaluation, governance and adoption, not fine-tuning a foundation model. The point is simpler: AI creates a new layer of work above the subscription, and the partners best placed to capture it are the ones who know the customer’s business well enough to make that layer valuable.

Futurum Research’s 2H 2026 partner survey found that 71% of active partners named custom application development as a primary growth driver, even as sentiment toward packaged enterprise software weakened. But that does not mean every bespoke build will be profitable. It does suggest that customers are looking beyond generic software for tailored engineering and that partners see more room in services than in a shrinking resale margin.

For SaaS founders, that changes the question from “How do we get partners to refer more deals?” to “What can partners build profitably with us?” Start by running the full math: referral and renewal income, plus the gross profit from partner-delivered implementation and AI services, minus the cost of acquiring and serving the account. If a partner can create a healthy contribution margin while making the product more useful to the customer, the program has a foundation. If it cannot, a higher referral percentage is just a more expensive version of the same problem.

The program should then make that work easier to do well. Give capable partners a sandbox that resembles production, not just a demo login. Train them on integration, evaluation, governance and escalation — not only on product features. Certify them against real use cases. Bring the strongest partners into the harder solutions early, before the vendor has decided every implementation detail in-house. That is how a platform becomes a place where partners can build expertise instead of merely resell a discount.

Measure the result accordingly. Referred ARR still matters, but it is only part of the picture. Track services revenue and margin where they can be observed, time to production, active use, product adoption, support burden, retention and the customer outcome the solution was designed to improve. Outcome-based incentives can work, too, if they are tied to milestones the partner can actually influence: a verified deployment, adoption by an agreed user group, a successful evaluation or a retained account after a defined period.

None of this removes the need for discipline. A vendor still needs clear data rights, guardrails, support boundaries and a view of who is accountable when a workflow fails. Partners need room to earn services revenue without creating a maintenance burden the vendor cannot support. Those are not reasons to stay with the old model. They are the operating details that turn the AI thesis into a business model.

The point is not that AI work will never commoditize. Some of it will, and it should. The point is that AI gives partners a larger, more defensible role while the work still depends on customer data, workflow knowledge and practical judgment. A program built around that role is harder to reduce to a commission table. It gives partners more reason to invest, gives customers more value from the platform, and gives the vendor something more durable than a better percentage to compete on.

#5473. Alta raises $48 million for its compliance-focused blockchain in Series A round led by Index Ventures

Financial firms looking to accelerate money transfers with crypto have no shortage of options when it comes to blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche. That hasn’t deterred a startup called Alta from trying to lure banks and big companies with a blockchain of its own. The chain seeks to stand out with its plug-and-play compliance layer that lets customers ensure that any transactions they process are consistent with rules and regulations anywhere in the world.

On Tuesday, Alta announced it has raised a $47.5 million a Series A round at an undisclosed valuation. The new round, which was led by Index Ventures, comes after the startup raised $32.5 million in seed funding backed primarily by the Australian fintech giant Airwallex, which is taking on Stripe and others in the global payments space.

The CEO of Alta is Loong Wang, who founded an earlier crypto startup that he sold in 2021, and then pivoted to a second startup that employs quantum computing to aid in drug discovery. Wang returned to crypto technology to found Alta, which recently rebranded from its original name of Metal, alongside former Meta executive Catherine Porter, who helped oversee the company’s since-abandoned crypto venture.

“We often say we wouldn’t have built an L-1 if we didn’t have to,” said Wang, noting that Alta’s features include one that prevents random people from sending funds to those with an address on the blockchain. (Most blockchains allow for so-called “airdrops” that oblige wallet holders to accept funds whether they want to or not).

Alta, which has 25 employees and offices in San Francisco and Melbourne, is also notable for its close ties to Airwallex. Those ties include a personal connection between Wang and Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang, who was a crypto skeptic, but recently acknowledged the inherent value of stablecoins when it comes to cheap and efficient money transfers.

Airwallex is also serving as a massive distribution channel for Alta, persuading its global network of customers to use the startup’s platform for crypto transactions. This comes at a time when Airwallex’s main rivals, including Stripe and its Tempo blockchain, are likewise building out crypto infrastructure.

“With the rise of agentic banking and programmable payments, stablecoins are becoming an important vector for settlement,” said Zhang in a statement announcing Alta’s latest funding round.

Also participating in the Series A funding round were GV (Google Ventures), Blackbird Ventures, Square Peg and Capital49, a venture firm established by Airwallex’s cofounders.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.
