#5472. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5471. You Don’t Need a Full-Time Executive to Get C-Suite Expertise. Here’s Why.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis — but it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Hiring full-time workers is a commitment, especially at the C-suite level. As a solopreneur myself, it took me a long time before I had the resources to bring anyone on to help shoulder the responsibilities of running my business.

But a lot has changed since I launched my company back in 2006. Now, fractional executives—leaders who share their expertise with organizations on a part-time basis—are quickly becoming the norm. In fact, research has found that the number of workers describing themselves as “fractional” has tripled since 2018; among executives, the most common limited roles are CFOs, followed by CMOs.

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis. The right fractional executive can bring valuable expertise, fresh perspective and strategic guidance without requiring the long-term investment of a full-time hire. But it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

Several factors have conspired to create the recent boom in fractional work. Post-Covid-19, more people are seeking out flexible roles and the ability to work multiple part-time jobs. At the same time, a tough job market has produced a surplus of highly skilled workers, while many companies don’t have the funds to fill those roles full-time.

Leadership roles are also simply growing more complex. Between the proliferation of hybrid work and AI adoption, it stands to reason that expertise is also becoming more varied. In general, high level roles are changing, with AI automating several functions previously handled by executives, like operations and reporting. On the other hand, demand for a la carte, specialized skills are on the rise — maybe your organization needs someone fluent in transitioning to an AI-powered workforce, but only on a limited-time basis.

You’d be forgiven for thinking fractional executives are just consultants by another, buzzier name. But the truth is they’re quite different.

The main distinction is that, while they do work on a part-time basis, fractional executives are embedded in your team. They make decisions that drive outcomes and are responsible for what happens as a result.

Consultants, on the other hand, operate outside the organization. They make recommendations, but are not ultimately accountable for how things turn out. For example, a consultant can analyze your pricing strategy and show you a presentation on how they think it can be improved. A fractional CFO, on the other hand, will rebuild the pricing model themselves, and answer for the numbers at the quarter’s end.

Before you hire someone touting themselves as a fractional executive, dig into the details of what they’re offering and make sure they — and you — understand the difference.

Fractional work may be a product of our current moment, but it’s also unlikely to go away any time soon.

For entrepreneurs, the perks of such roles are many. Benefits packages, equity and long-term salary commitments are not part of the equation. You get the expertise without the long-term overhead, and you can scale the relationship up or down as your needs change.

But fractional isn’t free of tradeoffs, and it isn’t right for every role. Start by asking a few questions:

It’s entirely possible that a fractional hire can turn into a full-time offer once the time is right. But understanding the role, its limitations and whether it’s the appropriate fit for your business is key. A fractional hire doesn’t need to feel like a compromise, because it shouldn’t be. Handled correctly, it’s a deliberate way to get the right expertise at the right time, without pretending your company needs something it doesn’t.

Hiring full-time workers is a commitment, especially at the C-suite level. As a solopreneur myself, it took me a long time before I had the resources to bring anyone on to help shoulder the responsibilities of running my business.

The right fractional executive can bring valuable expertise, fresh perspective and strategic guidance without requiring the long-term investment of a full-time hire. But it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

#5470. Meet the 27-year-old former firefighter who left Goldman to build a used-truck marketplace that’s now valued at $225 million

Martin Hunt joined the volunteer fire service at 15 in his corner of northern Delaware, just outside Philadelphia. Along with fighting fires, he eventually took on a less glamorous part of keeping a department running: selling its old trucks.

It was a lot harder than it sounds. A department that buys a new engine often needs to sell the one it replaced to help pay for it. However, finding a buyer meant cold-calling departments across the country or sending the truck to a local auction, where a vehicle that another town could use might unfortunately go for scrap.

Last year, the very same engine that carried Hunt to his first fire went up for sale. His hometown department’s board hoped to get $30,000. Instead, it sold within days for $125,000, Hunt said, on the online marketplace he had built with his cofounder, Alaz Sengul.

Their company, Garage, is building a nationwide marketplace for the trucks that keep communities running. It connects departments ready to sell with buyers who can’t afford new equipment or wait years for it to arrive, because a truck one town has replaced can still have a long working life somewhere else.

Now the 27-year-old former firefighter, who later worked in private equity at Goldman Sachs, has raised $41 million to grow it. The Series B, led by Invus Opportunities, values the startup at $225 million and brings its total funding to $60 million, the company told Fortune.

By 2023, Hunt was a private equity investor at Goldman Sachs when a friend from his old fire department reached out. The friend had taken over Hunt’s equipment duties and wanted to know how Hunt had managed to make it look so easy.

“I told him it wasn’t easy. I just didn’t complain a ton,” Hunt said.

Not much had changed since Hunt did the job nearly a decade earlier. Departments still leaned on auctions and word of mouth, and new trucks had only gotten harder to come by. Instead, Hunt said new truck can cost millions of dollars and take years to arrive.

The call got Hunt and Sengul, whom he met through a mutual friend at Columbia University, thinking about whether those sales could move online. Sengul had worked as a software engineer at Twitter (now X) and later at the AI note-taking startup Mem, while Hunt knew firsthand what the departments they hoped to serve were up against.

So they quit their jobs with no funding and no product, living off their savings as they built Garage. After joining Y Combinator’s winter 2024 batch, they moved to San Francisco and launched the marketplace early that year.

Garage doesn’t own the trucks, and there’s no lot full of fire engines waiting for buyers. Vehicles stay with their sellers until someone buys them, then go straight to their new home, which is often a long drive away. More than 90% of transactions cross state lines, Hunt said, and the average piece of equipment travels 1,400 miles.

Moving an 80,000-pound truck across the country takes more than a “buy now” button. Garage uses AI tools that appraise equipment and coordinate freight, and buyers anywhere in the lower 48 states can punch in a ZIP code for an instant delivery quote. The company also offers financing and optional warranties.

Hunt compares it to adding a T-shirt to your Amazon cart: buyers know the price, the shipping cost, and when it will show up. The goal, he said, is “an experience that feels a lot more like an Amazon than a Craigslist,” even when the item in the cart weighs tens of thousands of pounds and costs hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Still, a fire truck isn’t a T-shirt. Buyers can trade inspection reports with sellers and book video walkarounds, but buying anything used carries risk. “At the end of the day, they’re buying a used trash truck or a used fire truck, and so things do go wrong,” Hunt said.

Garage says it serves more than 1,000 communities across all 50 states and Canada. Hunt said equipment sales through the platform top $100 million on an annualized basis. The company makes money by charging sellers a 10% success fee on buy-now purchases and buyers a 10% premium at auction. Garage did not disclose its revenue.

For sellers, a bigger pool of buyers can mean real money. South Charleston, West Virginia, budgeted a few hundred thousand dollars from surplus sales in 2025 and instead brought in $1.2 million through Garage, Hunt said. The windfall helped pay for replacement equipment and firefighter cancer screenings.

“An extra million dollars has a real impact on a community,” Hunt said in a statement to Fortune. “Those funds can be reinvested in schools, roads, and local employees without increasing the burden on taxpayers.”

Burlington, Vermont, had previously sold surplus fire equipment through local auctions, often with little to show for it, Fire Chief Michael LaChance said in a testimonial on Garage’s website.

“Basically, we’d take what we could get, which wasn’t much,” he said.

After using Garage, LaChance said, “We got about five times more for our equipment selling with Garage than we did on our own.” According to the company, the proceeds will help replace the department’s command vehicle.

The new funding will go toward hiring and expanding into public works and sanitation. Fire trucks, it turns out, aren’t the only rigs looking for a second life; private sanitation companies are already Garage’s fastest-growing customer segment, Hunt said.

Even in fire, where Garage calls itself the largest source of used trucks in the country, Hunt estimates the company works with about 1% of the market.

“Even in our largest categories, we have a long way to go,” Hunt said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#5469. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5468. California Wine Country Saw Its Earliest Harvest in Decades. Here’s How a 67-Year-Old Business Navigated It — And What Every Entrepreneur Can Learn.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From supply chain to sustainability, Rodney Strong Vineyards knows what it takes to succeed.

Napa Valley and Sonoma, two of California’s top-growing wine regions, recently underwent their earliest grape harvest in decades. In response to a record-breaking March heat wave and early bud break, grape-picking started in July. The process typically starts in early to mid-August.

Fortunately, wine-growers and -makers across the region turn to harvest playbooks that have withstood the test of time.

One of them is 67-year-old Rodney Strong Vineyards in Healdsburg, California.

Rodney Strong, who had a brief stint in the Navy before dancing on Broadway in New York City, retired from performing life and established his namesake winery in 1959. He brought on Rick Sayre as winemaker in 1979.

In 1989, the Klein family purchased Rodney Strong Vineyards. A graduate of Stanford’s MBA program, Tom Klein met Strong and Sayre a decade prior when his team at McKinsey & Company was hired to evaluate the winery.

To this day, more than six decades on, a successful harvest at Rodney Strong Vineyards strikes the balance between art and science. (Just one example of many: The preferred light pink shade of Rodney Strong’s rosé requires bringing those grapes in under the cover of night, before any heat can degrade them).

During the final days of 2026’s harvest, Entrepreneur visited Rodney Strong Vineyards and its estate vineyard Rockaway Vineyards to learn more about the business’s approach.

The takeaways from chief winemaking and operations officer Justin Seidenfeld and head of winegrowing Allison Dericco can ripen any business for success, whether or not they’re focused on the vine.

Businesses should never underestimate the value of knowing their supply chain — and its nuances — to ensure their product delivers on quality every time.

On the topic of Rodney Strong’s very intentional rosé: Heat is the most immediate logistical risk to grape quality between a morning harvest at Rockaway Vineyards and the crush pad.

“As the fruit sits in the sun, it will begin to dessicate,” Seidenfeld says. “That will change the balance of the fruit.”

That’s why the team starts picking grapes at dawn and fast tracks them to the winery. The fruit is kept in an air-conditioned space until it’s sorted and put into a tank for fermentation, Seidenfeld notes.

These days, businesses across industries can drill down on their supply chain with advanced technologies that gather data at every touchpoint, putting an innovative twist on operational fundamentals that comes with a major competitive advantage.

In a similar vein, businesses have to understand their assets and how to prioritize them for long-term success.

Rodney Strong boasts a robust wine portfolio. A premium, small-lot Rockaway grape experiences a different crush and fermentation than a larger-lot grape destined for the broader Sonoma County or Estate tiers.

Rodney Strong’s Sonoma and Estate wines are larger, so they require a less precise “sweet spotting” technique compared to Rockaway and other reserve wines, Seidenfeld says.

Still, those grapes destined for the broader tier are managed closely to ensure quality.

“[We rely on] careful site development to keep the block as uniform as possible and the implantation of deficit irrigation to help find as much balance across the whole block as possible,” Seidenfeld says.

What’s more, any business can put this into practice by zeroing in on an often overlooked strategy: dynamic resource allocation, which shifts money, talent and management attention to areas where they can generate the most value.

Data analysis plays an important role in business operations and risk mitigation, but well-informed intuition can be just as valuable.

At the vineyard, whether a block of grapes hangs on the vine for one more day or gets picked as soon as possible comes down to chemistry and gut feeling.

Seidenfeld says the decision on when to harvest is the most important one the winery makes every year.

“While we use the data from the samples we pull to guide us, the final call on when to harvest is made through our eyes and ears and taste and not with what we get from the lab,” Seidenfeld explains.

Some degree of risk is inevitable in business, but entrepreneurs who pay attention to the pressures related to growth, culture and information management can sharpen their decision-making ability when it counts — and minimize potential losses.

Businesses that embrace sustainability not only foster positive consumer sentiment, but also protect their long-term product viability and bottom line.

Rodney Strong became the first carbon neutral winery in Sonoma County in 2009. The team works to create a balanced growing environment with practices like water conservation, soil management and biodiversity encouragement, maintaining healthy vines and managing stress as they develop, Dericco notes.

Additionally, using tools like soil moisture monitoring, weather stations and plant-based measurements allows the team to make more precise farming decisions, particularly when it comes to irrigation.

“While our carbon neutrality and waste reduction efforts have broader environmental benefits, it’s these everyday practices in the vineyard that directly influence vine health, fruit development, and ultimately, wine quality,” Dericco says.

The lesson for business owners? Consider sustainability a building block, not an afterthought, to ensure genuine messaging and meaningful collaboration.

#5467. After a summer of reorganizing national debt, the Treasury borrowed more than $100 billion a week in October

The fiscal year of 2027 is not off to a great start for the U.S. Treasury’s pocket book.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) just released its October budget report, the first month of the 2027 fiscal calendar year.

The strictly nonpartisan CBO reported that in October 2026, it estimated the federal government incurred a deficit of $409 billion—more than $100 billion a week. This is $125 billion more than the shortfall recorded last October.

Revenues were $36 billion lower, and outlays were $89 billion higher than the same month last year, according to the CBO. The report suggested October’s federal deficit was that much higher due to shifts in the timing of certain federal payments that otherwise would have been made on November 1 (that date fell on a weekend in 2025 and 2026, therefore pushing those payments into October of each year).

This comes after a summer of debt reshuffling in the U.S. Treasury, with fiscal hawks questioning whether Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was moving deckchairs on the Titanic, rather than meaningfully improving the macroeconomic picture.

Bessent described this summer’s actions as a “Treasury twist,” a reference to policymaker action in which longer-dated Treasuries are bought and paid for by issuing shorter-term debt. The strategy has not been confirmed verbatim by the Treasury, but Bessent himself has indicated the scheme worked by buying back more expensive, long-term debt (in which yields, and hence interest, are higher) in lieu of cheaper, short-term debt.

The move did not impress markets. JPMorgan’s co-head of global fundamental research, James Sullivan, described it as “paying your mortgage with your credit card. It can work for a while, but eventually the mismatch starts to become more obvious.”

Context has since achieved the desired effect: A range of factors (including tough Fed talk on inflation and the recent AI rout) have brought down longer-dated yields and smoothed volatility.

While this has made government borrowing relatively cheaper in the long term (interest rates are tied to long-dated Treasury yields), it will do little to reassure debt hawks the U.S. fiscal trajectory is on a sustainable path.

In its budget review, the CBO showed that for the fiscal year of 2026, the deficit was at 6.2% of the nation’s GDP, up from 5.8% a year prior. This percentage is greater than the 50-year average of 3.8%, and has only previously been matched or exceeded eight times since 1946: from 2009 through 2012 and in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

The total deficit for the year was $1.9 trillion, the CBO added, with $1.14 trillion spent on interest on the public debt.

Government income was up for the year to $5.4 trillion, up $169 billion in the 2025 fiscal year, thanks, in large part, to increases in collections of individual income and payroll taxes. But, on the contrary, total outlays increased by $217 billion—most of which came from an uptick in Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5466. Students Want More Than Degrees. Community Colleges Now Have to Prove Economic Value

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Community colleges are rethinking student success by focusing on living-wage jobs and higher earnings.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Students are increasingly looking beyond earning a college degree or credential. They want to know whether their education will lead to meaningful employment, better earnings, and long-term career opportunities. As expectations shift toward tangible career outcomes, community colleges are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value of the programs they offer.

A July 2026 report from the Aspen Institute and Columbia University’s Community College Research Center highlights the challenge. According to the research, more than one-third of community college credentials are unlikely to lead directly to living-wage jobs or bachelor’s degrees that provide pathways to such employment. This raises an important question: Are colleges preparing students simply to complete academic programs, or to succeed in the workforce?

Some institutions are already rethinking their approach. Through the Unlocking Opportunity initiative, launched in 2022, 10 community colleges across the United States have been working to align academic programs more closely with employment opportunities and pathways to further education. Between 2022 and 2025, these institutions moved more than 20,000 additional students into programs associated with stronger career and transfer outcomes, representing a 27% increase in enrollment in high-value pathways.

These developments point to a shift in how community colleges are defining student success, placing greater emphasis on the career opportunities and economic mobility that education can create.

As students increasingly prioritize career outcomes, community colleges are reassessing whether their academic programs reflect labor market needs. Rather than relying solely on enrollment demand or existing course offerings, institutions are using employment data, regional workforce trends, and employer partnerships to identify programs that can lead to stronger career opportunities.

This approach is particularly important in sectors facing workforce shortages, where colleges can play a direct role in preparing students for in-demand occupations. By collaborating with employers, institutions can better understand the skills required for specific roles, adapt their curricula, and expand access to practical training opportunities.

At San Antonio College in Texas, this strategy has translated into measurable enrollment growth. To address a regional nursing shortage, the college partnered with healthcare employers to expand clinical training placements, a major constraint on nursing program capacity. According to the Aspen Institute’s July 2026 report, these efforts helped increase enrollment in its selective nursing programs by 71% over three years.

Similarly, Southwest Wisconsin Technical College identified a shortage of radiologic technologists in its region and introduced a radiography program to address the gap. Local hospitals supported the initiative by donating equipment, while the college converted existing space into a training laboratory. The program filled its available places upon launch, demonstrating student demand for training connected to regional employment opportunities.

These examples show how community colleges are taking a more active role in workforce development. Instead of simply offering programs and leaving students to navigate the job market after graduation, institutions are collaborating with employers to create clearer pathways into in-demand occupations. While the long-term employment outcomes of these initiatives are still being evaluated, their early results demonstrate how aligning academic offerings with workforce needs can expand access to career-oriented education.

As the value of higher education comes under greater scrutiny, community colleges are facing a difficult question: Should they continue offering programs that attract students but provide limited opportunities after graduation? Enrollment and completion rates remain important indicators of institutional performance, but they do not necessarily reflect the economic value of a credential.

This is prompting a closer examination of how academic programs align with employment opportunities, graduate earnings, and pathways to further education. Rather than evaluating programs solely on student demand, colleges can use labor market information and graduate outcomes to determine which offerings need to be updated, expanded, or reconsidered.

South Puget Sound Community College in Washington offers a recent example. In 2026, the college’s board voted to close its Paralegal, Culinary Arts, and Baking & Pastry Arts programs following a review of regional employment demand, career outcomes, and financial sustainability. College officials found that many local culinary and baking positions did not require formal qualifications or offer significant wage advantages to credential holders. The decision was also driven by budgetary pressures, with the two food-related programs costing the institution approximately $618,000 annually.

However, measuring program value is not always straightforward. Some credentials prepare students for immediate employment, while others provide foundational education for transfer to four-year institutions. A program with modest short-term earnings may still offer significant long-term value if it helps students pursue advanced qualifications or enter occupations with stronger career progression.

For community colleges, the challenge is not simply to eliminate programs with weaker employment outcomes. It is to ensure that students understand where different educational pathways can lead and that institutions regularly assess whether their offerings deliver on those expectations.

Helping students enter programs with strong career prospects requires more than offering the right courses. Community colleges are increasingly integrating career planning into academic advising to help students understand employment opportunities, potential earnings, and the qualifications needed for their chosen careers.

A 2024 report from the Center for Community College Student Engagement, based on responses from 83,189 students across 199 community colleges, found that more than 90% had chosen a career path, yet many lacked essential information about how to pursue it.

To address this gap, Lane Community College in Oregon uses a Guided Pathways framework to help students explore career options, select programs, and develop academic plans. Technology, including AI-supported advising tools, can further improve access to personalized guidance and help advisors identify students who need additional support.

By connecting academic decisions with career goals earlier, community colleges can help students make more informed choices about their education and future employment.

The path forward requires community colleges to turn these strategies into measurable results. Stronger employer partnerships, regular program evaluations, and proactive career advising must become integral to how institutions operate, rather than isolated initiatives.

The challenge now is to ensure that these changes translate into better employment prospects, higher earnings, and smoother transitions to further education. Ultimately, the institutions that succeed will be those that can demonstrate the economic value of their programs and consistently deliver on the career opportunities they promise students.

#5465. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5464. AI Is Making Expertise Cheaper. Here’s What Will Make You More Valuable.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When customers can access sophisticated knowledge through AI, entrepreneurs need to rethink what makes their expertise valuable.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, being an expert was a competitive advantage. You spent years developing knowledge, understanding an industry and accumulating experience that other people didn’t have. Customers paid for access to that expertise because acquiring it themselves was difficult, expensive or time-consuming.

Today, a business owner can ask AI to analyze a market, explain a financial concept or develop a marketing strategy, receiving information that previously might have required a specialist.

Knowing all the answers used to make you the smartest person in the room. Today, it might just make you the most expensive search engine. The uncomfortable question for entrepreneurs who sell expertise is this: If customers can access much of what you know, what exactly are they paying you for?

This isn’t simply a prediction about where AI might take us. We’re already seeing how knowledge-based work is changing. Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that 81% of leaders expected AI agents to be moderately or extensively integrated into their companies’ AI strategies within 12–18 months. Meanwhile, the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 identified analytical thinking as the most important core skill for employers, with creative thinking, resilience and technological literacy also featuring prominently.

These findings point toward an important distinction. Technology is becoming increasingly capable of producing information and completing tasks, but businesses still need people who can evaluate that information, connect it to commercial realities and decide what should happen next.

Consider a consultant who has spent 20 years becoming an expert in a particular industry. That knowledge hasn’t suddenly become worthless, but if much of their value proposition involves explaining information that AI can now provide in seconds, customers may reasonably question what they’re paying for. The premium is shifting from possessing knowledge to applying it.

I founded my international public relations agency, NettResults, in 1999. At the time, one of our advantages was having specialist knowledge of the Middle East technology market. International companies entering the region needed to understand the media landscape, local business practices, cultural differences and how to communicate effectively with unfamiliar audiences. We had that knowledge, along with relationships that took years to develop. Clients couldn’t simply search for much of the information or replicate those relationships overnight.

Today, AI can explain the regional media landscape, identify publications, research competitors and help develop communications strategies in minutes. Information that once took considerable time and experience to assemble is increasingly accessible, but that doesn’t mean our expertise has become less valuable. Knowing which publications cover technology is useful. Knowing which journalist is likely to care about a particular story, how regional sensitivities might affect its reception and whether the story should be pitched at all requires something different. It requires experience, relationships, context and judgment — and those are much harder to automate.

One limitation of traditional expertise is that we tend to organize it into disciplines. Marketing people understand marketing, financial people understand finance, and technology specialists understand technology. But business problems rarely arrive neatly labeled, and solving them often requires looking beyond the area where the symptoms first appear.

I recently worked with a business owner who believed he needed to hire more people because his company was struggling to keep up with demand. On the surface, it was a staffing problem. But as we examined the business, we discovered that inefficient processes, unclear responsibilities and the owner’s involvement in too many everyday decisions were creating much of the pressure. Hiring more employees might have increased capacity, but it wouldn’t necessarily have solved the underlying problem. The better approach was to examine workflows, clarify accountability and identify where technology could remove unnecessary work before adding more people.

What initially looked like a hiring decision was actually a combination of operational design, leadership and technology. AI can help analyze each of those areas, but the entrepreneur’s opportunity is to connect them, recognize which information matters and make decisions that account for the whole business. The business owner who understands enough about technology, psychology, finance, operations and customer behavior to connect those disciplines may create more value than someone who knows everything about just one of them.

That doesn’t mean specialists are becoming unnecessary. Deep expertise remains essential, particularly when decisions carry significant financial, legal or operational consequences. But expertise without the ability to apply it in context becomes easier to commoditize.

If your business sells knowledge, advice or specialist services, I recommend examining how your value proposition is changing. This doesn’t require an expensive consultant or a six-month strategic review. Start by asking four questions about what your customers actually buy from you and where you create value that they cannot easily reproduce themselves.

1. What do customers currently pay us to know? Identify the specialist knowledge, information and capabilities that underpin your products or services.

2. What could AI now provide them directly? Be realistic about which parts of your offering are becoming easier, faster or cheaper for customers to access independently.

3. Where does our judgment create value? Look for the decisions, relationships, interpretation and experience that produce better outcomes than information alone.

4. How should we reposition what we sell? Consider whether you should be charging for access to knowledge, time spent delivering it or the commercial outcomes your expertise helps customers achieve.

This exercise isn’t about abandoning your expertise. It’s about making sure you’re not building tomorrow’s business around yesterday’s competitive advantage.

For entrepreneurs, the opportunity isn’t to compete with AI on how much information we can produce. That’s a competition we’re unlikely to win. Instead, we need to become better at asking the right questions, connecting information across disciplines and making decisions that create measurable value for customers.

AI can increasingly tell people what is possible. Experienced entrepreneurs and professionals help determine what is sensible, commercially viable and worth doing. The future doesn’t belong to people who simply know the most. It belongs to those who know what matters, what to do about it and are prepared to take responsibility for the result.

For decades, being an expert was a competitive advantage. You spent years developing knowledge, understanding an industry and accumulating experience that other people didn’t have. Customers paid for access to that expertise because acquiring it themselves was difficult, expensive or time-consuming.

Today, a business owner can ask AI to analyze a market, explain a financial concept or develop a marketing strategy, receiving information that previously might have required a specialist.

Knowing all the answers used to make you the smartest person in the room. Today, it might just make you the most expensive search engine. The uncomfortable question for entrepreneurs who sell expertise is this: If customers can access much of what you know, what exactly are they paying you for?

#5463. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5462. Solana Targets Durable Nonces After $270M Drift Hack as Pump.fun Backlash Grows

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Solana developers are preparing to remove durable nonces, the transaction feature exploited in April’s $270 million Drift Protocol hack. The proposed change marks a major shift in how the network handles offline approvals, with implications for exchanges and institutional custodians.

The proposal, known as SIMD-0723, would retire a mechanism that allows signed transactions to remain valid indefinitely. Attackers reportedly exploited this functionality to execute pre-approved transactions more than a week after obtaining signatures from Drift’s security council.

Solana wants to kill the feature behind April's $270M+ Drift hack.SIMD-0723, filed Nov 5 by Anza, would retire "durable nonces": signed transactions that never expire. Normal Solana transactions go stale in ~30 seconds. Earliest switch-off: May 5, 2027. pic.twitter.com/VYYttCsvJk

The move comes as Solana faces another challenge closer to its retail ecosystem. Pump.fun is facing growing community criticism over platform fees, influencer promotions, and allegations of hidden-wallet trading. Together, the developments put renewed attention on security, transparency and trust across Solana’s ecosystem.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Normal Solana transactions use recent blockhashes that expire after 30 seconds. Durable nonces replace those temporary references with stored values, allowing transactions to remain executable until the nonce advances.

The feature was designed for legitimate operational needs. Exchanges, custodians, and multisig organizations often require offline signing procedures that take longer than Solana’s normal transaction window.

However, attackers turned that convenience into an attack vector against Drift on April 1, 2026. They reportedly secured administrative approvals through air-gapped signing systems before allowing the transactions to sit for more than a week.

Once submitted, the approvals helped attackers take control of the protocol and drain at least $270 million. Drift subsequently attributed the attack to a North Korean-linked group.

Anza contributor Gabe Rodriguez filed SIMD-0723 on November 5. The proposal would require transactions to use recent blockhashes after activation. May 5, 2027, represents the earliest proposed mainnet activation date. The change still requires technical approval and migration planning.

Solana is also exploring replacement programs that could support offline signing without relying on durable nonces. These alternatives would introduce different authorization and transaction-failure considerations for custodians.

The proposal forces institutional users to reconsider how they authorize transactions across Solana. Meanwhile, questions about trust are becoming harder to ignore elsewhere in the ecosystem.

Pump.fun has attracted fresh criticism following several developments involving its business model and influencer ecosystem.

On November 6, blockchain tracker Lookonchain reported that Pump.fun transferred 76,111 SOL, worth approximately $6.85 million, to Kraken. The movement reignited criticism over platform fees and whether its incentives adequately serve ordinary traders.

Bubblemaps also accused prominent influencers of using undisclosed wallets to purchase tokens before publicly recommending them. Its investigations estimated $125,000 in combined trading profits and promotional rewards involving influencer Ethan.

Separate allegations involving paid streamer collaborations surfaced on November 7. The revelations have intensified questions about transparency within Pump.fun’s promotional ecosystem.

These controversies involve different problems from Drift’s exploit, but they expose a similar challenge: maintaining confidence among participants.

Bitcoin Hyper is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 using Solana Virtual Machine technology. Its architecture aims to combine SVM’s high-speed execution with Bitcoin-based settlement, bringing smart contracts, decentralized exchanges, and staking functionality to BTC.

Bitcoin Hyper is not simply another Solana application. Its design uses SVM execution while anchoring Layer 2 state to Bitcoin through periodic commitments and zero-knowledge proofs.

This combination gives it a different proposition from Solana-native applications. Developers can work with an execution environment associated with Solana’s performance, while the project targets Bitcoin’s established settlement infrastructure.

#5461. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5460. It’s Time to Confront the Realities of What Your CRM Can Do — and What It Can’t

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

CRMs can be powerful tools, but they’re not crystal balls.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In the world of franchise recruitment, nothing is more sacred than a quality lead. And at any given time, there are potentially millions of Americans considering an entrepreneurial future, some of whom have always harbored a desire to own and operate a business of their own and others for whom circumstances dictated taking matters into their own hands. Both of these would-be entrepreneurial types are invaluable, as you never know which one may go on to sign an official franchise agreement.

That means tracking every lead is paramount. The majority of franchise sales and development teams are highly reliant on their Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems to achieve this important task. Thanks to today’s technologies, now fully integrated with the power of AI, CRM databases have become much more complex in both design and functionality. Much thought and consideration go into these factors, providing development teams with what they hope will be an efficient roadmap to meet their outsized recruitment goals.

But there’s a catch. Regardless of how much time, capital and manpower sales and development teams pour into their proprietary CRM systems, they’re not exactly infallible. And that’s where the true issue lies. Accepting this reality means you understand the limitations, making now as good a time as any to confront the reality of what your CRM can do.

Whether you’re starting from scratch or looking to upgrade your CRM’s capabilities, there are some essential factors to consider in finding the right fit for your organization. Ideally, you’re looking to establish a critical technological component of your franchise recruitment effort, a centralized database of candidates that will come to define your “quantity vs. quality” approach.

When assessing your specific needs in a CRM, there are several rhetorical questions involved. But regardless of your organization’s size or its recruitment strategy, your CRM should be designed with long-term value in mind. Here is what’s most important to consider if you want to get started on the right foot:

Once you’ve defined these critical components, your sales and development team is ready to progress to the procurement stage. This is not the time to scrimp on your due diligence, so take the necessary time to evaluate your CRM options and pay close attention to the demos offered by different technology providers.

The very title of this article establishes that CRMs are not the panacea for your franchise recruitment efforts. That’s because, despite the advanced automated capabilities baked into the most technologically advanced CRM, there are still things it cannot accomplish for you. These can be broken down into three key areas:

1. Activity tracking does not guarantee pipeline health

By design, the majority of advanced CRM setups are designed to capture data, manage incoming leads and keep track of real-time updates and activity. And they do a fine job with these capabilities — but what they can’t do is provide your sales and development teams with the predictive analytics necessary to make informed decisions on how to proceed. In other words, it can’t inherently show you the health and viability of your current sales pipeline.

2. Critical datasets may be siloed elsewhere

Even with the most advanced capabilities, including those powered by AI, CRMs can’t truly assess the total investment you’ve made in front-end lead generation and tie that back to long-term backend performance. That’s because the valuable insights you need to make informed decisions may not be readily available in the CRM, but scattered across other networks … even external ones.

In a typical knee-jerk reaction, franchise sales and development teams that miss the mark on their intended recruiting goals immediately go into finger-pointing mode. When signings fall short, the CRM often gets the blame. Before replacing it, examine how your team defines the process, maintains the data and follows through with candidates. But the issue here is franchise development teams mistaking their CRM as a structural sales methodology, when in fact success calls for a more disciplined, human-centric approach.

Franchise recruitment teams can be quick to blame CRM systems when their lead-generation goals go unmet. So, they take the most drastic action first and decide to change it out for something shinier, better and — in almost every instance — more expensive. But even after all those changes, and the requisite amount of time goes by, they find themselves in the exact same situation down the road.

That’s because the standards they’re applying to measure results aren’t where the actual problems lie. More often than not, the real problem is in how they’re utilizing the CRM system and what they’re asking it to accomplish.

By design, CRMs are powerful systems that do an admirable job doing exactly what we program them to do — to the letter. They track activity, manage leads, store critical information for later retrieval, and can provide us with real-time updates of where every candidate is in the process. They keep the pipeline moving smoothly and efficiently. But never mistake that for visibility or predictive analytics.

CRMs are not infallible, and they’re definitely not the crystal ball you’re looking for when it comes to predicting the long-term success of your franchise recruitment goals. Before you blame your CRM, take a hard look at your recruitment process, the quality of your data and who is accountable for moving each candidate forward.

In the world of franchise recruitment, nothing is more sacred than a quality lead. And at any given time, there are potentially millions of Americans considering an entrepreneurial future, some of whom have always harbored a desire to own and operate a business of their own and others for whom circumstances dictated taking matters into their own hands. Both of these would-be entrepreneurial types are invaluable, as you never know which one may go on to sign an official franchise agreement.

That means tracking every lead is paramount. The majority of franchise sales and development teams are highly reliant on their Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems to achieve this important task. Thanks to today’s technologies, now fully integrated with the power of AI, CRM databases have become much more complex in both design and functionality. Much thought and consideration go into these factors, providing development teams with what they hope will be an efficient roadmap to meet their outsized recruitment goals.

But there’s a catch. Regardless of how much time, capital and manpower sales and development teams pour into their proprietary CRM systems, they’re not exactly infallible. And that’s where the true issue lies. Accepting this reality means you understand the limitations, making now as good a time as any to confront the reality of what your CRM can do.

#5459. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

#5458. Coinbase Bank Gets Full OCC Approval as Ripple Leads Crypto Banking Push

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Coinbase has moved closer to the center of the US financial system after securing full approval for its national trust bank charter. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) recorded the charter as effective on November 6. The development gives Coinbase a federally supervised framework for expanding its institutional custody and digital asset services.

The approval completes a process that began with Coinbase’s application in October 2025. The OCC granted conditional approval on April 2, 2026, before recording the charter as consummated. Coinbase can now operate through its national trust company under federal supervision.

Coinbase follows Ripple’s final OCC approval on October 26. Two major crypto companies have now secured national trust bank charters within weeks. Their progress shows how digital asset firms are increasingly seeking access to regulated financial infrastructure rather than operating outside traditional banking frameworks.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Coinbase’s approval follows a similar regulatory path taken by Ripple. The company received conditional approval for Ripple National Trust Bank in December 2025. Its final approval arrived on October 26, completing the process ahead of Coinbase.

Ripple’s charter has specific implications for its stablecoin business. Ripple National Trust Bank can manage the segregated reserves backing RLUSD. It can also act as collateral trustee and provide fiduciary digital asset custody services.

RLUSD will continue to be issued by Standard Custody & Trust Company, Ripple’s New York-regulated trust company. The new federal charter adds another layer of supervision around its reserve management and institutional services.

Coinbase Bank has a different commercial opportunity. Its national trust company can provide federally supervised custody and fiduciary services to institutional clients. Coinbase previously said the charter would support its Prime custody business and other regulated services.

The growing number of crypto trust bank approvals has not gone unchallenged. The Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) filed a lawsuit against the OCC on October 2. The group argues that the regulator exceeded its authority by expanding access to national trust charters.

The banking association claims crypto companies receive federal banking credibility without meeting several requirements imposed on traditional banks. These include FDIC insurance, certain capital and liquidity standards, and Community Reinvestment Act obligations.

🚨 BIG: ICBA Sues OCC Over Crypto Trust Bank ChartersThe Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) has sued the OCC, arguing that its rules allowing crypto firms to obtain national trust bank charters exceed the agency’s legal authority and do not impose the same… pic.twitter.com/kJ8fVcXPoj

The lawsuit challenges the OCC’s March 2026 rule and related guidance. It argues that the regulator has stretched the national trust charter beyond its original statutory purpose.

The dispute could have consequences beyond Coinbase and Ripple. A successful challenge could complicate the regulatory pathway for other digital asset companies pursuing similar charters.

However, the OCC’s approach reflects a wider shift in US financial regulation. The agency has increasingly opened the door to crypto custody, payments, and stablecoin-related activities under federal supervision. This shift also creates opportunities for emerging blockchain infrastructure projects.

Coinbase Bank’s approval represents more than another regulatory milestone. It shows that crypto companies are competing for a larger role in the financial infrastructure institutions will use.
